docs.x: Multi-Agent Orchestration. Choose the orchestration pattern a production workload needs, draw the delegation and context-isolation boundaries, make agents communicate through structured handoffs, and place approval gates where they stop only the action that needs a person.

A multi-agent system is a set of model contexts that hand work to each other. Each context starts with only what it is given. That single fact explains most production failures: duplicated work, lost findings, claims that lose their sources, and approvals that block more than they should. The exam describes a running system, shows you the evidence from its traces, and asks which change fixes the failure.

docs.h: The patterns and when they earn their cost
docs.x: Pattern Shape Fits when Watch for Supervisor and workers A coordinator splits the task, workers each do one part, the coordinator merges The parts are independent and the merge is well defined Vague task messages; free-text results the merge misreads Parallel subagent dispatch Many workers run at once on separate slices Breadth-first research, partitioned search Over-spawning, hung workers, silent gaps Handoff between agents One agent finishes its part and passes the conversation on Distinct stages with different tools or policies Re-asking for facts already verified; huge transcripts Single agent with tools One context, possibly with subagents for isolated lookups Steps depend on each other Context growth on long tasks Parallel agents cost several times the tokens of a single agent for the same task. They pay off only when the work divides into pieces whose intermediate steps the coordinator does not need to see. Delegate to a subagent when only the result matters to the main thread. Keep the work in one context when each step depends on what the previous one discovered. Bug fixing (reproduce, diagnose, patch) almost always fails the test, because each step needs the details the last one learned.

A subagent starts with its own system prompt and the task message the coordinator writes, nothing more. If three subagents receive "research market trends in Asia-Pacific", they will overlap and miss things, whatever model they run. A good brief states: - the scope and what is out of scope, - the sources to prefer, - the output format, including a status field and an obstacles section, - the deadline or budget. In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, the subagent's description does double duty: the main agent reads it to decide when to delegate, and uses it as guidance when writing the task message. A description that says "the delegator must name the files to review and the criteria" produces specific briefs.

docs.c: The estimate that became a fact
docs.x: Free text between agents is the most common source of inter-agent failure. "Could not verify the policy number" can be merged as a pass. Use a schema: Field Why status (complete, partial, failed) The merge cannot mistake a failure for a finding findings with source and verified per claim Provenance survives synthesis obstacles Workarounds and errors reach the coordinator run_id Every worker span joins the coordinator's trace Pass a compact, structured record between agents, not the whole transcript. A mortgage specialist needs "identity verified at 10:42 by the intake agent", not 18,000 tokens of conversation. A research subagent's lookup failed. It wrote an estimate instead and did not report the error. The coordinator, reading prose, turned the estimate into a confident figure in a client report. Two changes fix the class of failure: the subagent returns each claim with its source and verification status as fields, and a check after synthesis rejects claims with no source.

When one context reads untrusted content (supplier websites, emails, tickets) and also holds a consequential tool (purchase orders, email, payments), any injected instruction can reach the tool. Split them: a read-only subagent processes the untrusted content and returns validated, structured fields; only the agent that never saw the raw text can act.

- Deadlines per worker, enforced by the harness, with one bounded retry or an alternate source. - Honest gaps: if a worker still fails, the final result states what is missing. Never let the coordinator fill a gap from its own knowledge. - Caps on fan-out: a per-run limit on subagents and tokens in the harness, plus guidance on how many subagents each kind of question warrants. A prompt regression should not be able to multiply cost tenfold. - Separate write targets: parallel agents that share a file system each write to their own path; the coordinator merges.

docs.c: "Tell the agent to ask first" · Managed Agents
docs.x: An approval gate belongs where the action happens, enforced in the tool or permission layer, not in the system prompt. It should: 1. stop only the action that needs a decision (one refund, one invoice), not the whole run; 2. give the approver what they need to decide: the action, the amount, the evidence; 3. have a timeout with a safe default when no one answers (for payments, decline); 4. leave a record of who approved what. Gating every action to control a few creates a queue that reviewers learn to rubber-stamp. Reviewing after the fact finds the bad refund after the money has left. A system-prompt instruction to request approval is advisory. A confused or injected turn can skip it. Exam answers that put the threshold in the prompt are almost always wrong when money or data is at stake. Claude Managed Agents provides multi-agent coordination, a shared file system per session, and permission policies that pause a tool call until it is approved. The same design rules apply: specialists write to their own paths, and sensitive actions wait for a person.

Orchestration items describe a running multi-agent system and a failure seen in traces: overlap, missing coverage, misread results, runaway cost, an exploit, or an approval bottleneck. Find the boundary where information or control was lost, then pick the change that fixes that boundary: a clearer brief, a schema, a run ID, an isolation split, a harness cap, or a narrowly placed gate. Distractors add more agents, bigger models, longer summaries, peer-to-peer chatter, or prompt instructions.

docs.h: Apply it: Restructure Granite's fraud-review agent
docs.x: Granite Federal Bank wants to split its fraud-review agent into a coordinator and specialists: one reads transaction history, one reads device and login data, and one reads the free-text memos and dispute messages customers write. The coordinator writes the case summary and can open or close cases. A red-team test already showed that a memo containing instructions could make the agent add an external email address to a case. 1. Decide which specialists should exist, and which tools each one gets. Why: the memo reader handles untrusted text. 2. Define the result schema every specialist returns to the coordinator. 3. Place the approval gates for closing a case and for any change to who is notified about a case. 4. Set the failure-containment rules for a specialist that times out. Done when: the coordinator can never publish a summary that silently omits an area. 1. Specialists and tools Specialist Tools Why Transactions get_transactions (read-only, scoped to the alert's account) Needs history, nothing else Device and login get_device_events (read-only) Same Memo reader No tools; returns structured fields only It reads untrusted customer text, so it must not reach anything that acts Only the coordinator can call open_case and close_case . No agent can call a tool that changes notification recipients; that becomes an analyst action in the case system. 2. Schema. status (complete, partial, failed), findings (each with source , timestamp , verified ), risk_signals (enumerated values), obstacles , run_id . The memo reader returns enumerated signals ("customer disputes merchant", "mentions travel") and a short quoted excerpt, never instructions. 3. Gates. Opening a case needs no approval. Closing a case as "not fraud" above a set amount pauses for an analyst, who sees the summary and the evidence. Notification changes are not an agent capability at all. 4. Containment. Each specialist has a deadline of 60 seconds and one retry. If a specialist still fails, the summary lists the missing area under "Not reviewed", the case stays open, and an analyst is assigned. - The context that reads untrusted text holds no tool that acts. - Results carry status, sources and a run ID, not free prose. - Gates are enforced in the tool layer and stop only the risky action. - A missing specialist produces a visible gap, not a guess.

Durable Execution and State Management. Keep long-running agents correct through crashes, disconnects, pauses and model changes by putting progress in durable state, resuming from checkpoints, making repeated side effects safe, and reading stop reasons as explicit run states.

An agent that runs for hours will be interrupted: containers are replaced, connections drop, approvals take days, snapshots retire. Durable execution means the run's progress lives outside the conversation , so a new process (or a new model) can pick up exactly where the old one stopped. The conversation is working memory; it is not a database.

docs.h: Four questions every long run must answer
docs.x: Question Durable answer Fragile answer What has been done? A journal or status file updated after each verified step The transcript, or the agent's own judgment Where do I resume? The last completed step in the journal The beginning Is repeating a step safe? An idempotency key from the business action on every side effect "Check your earlier messages first" Why did the run stop? The stop reason mapped to a recorded state "It printed something, so it must be done"

A checkpoint is what a new run needs to resume, not everything the old run saw. - Write at step boundaries, after a unit of work is verified (a report converted, a test passed). - Store compact state: the task, completed items, key findings, open questions. Keep large artifacts (tool outputs, files) in external storage and checkpoint references to them. - Make state machine-readable: a structured feature list with pass or fail per item, updated only after tests pass, tells each fresh session what is truly finished. Without it, new contexts either redo work or declare victory early. Serializing the full transcript every few seconds is slow to write and may not fit back into a context window. Compressing it does not fix either problem. If a fact must survive a restart, write it somewhere the harness reads on start. A summary in the final message is never written when the container dies mid-run.

Runtime Where session state lives What the application must do Messages API loop you write Wherever you store it Persist messages and your own step journal Agent SDK On the host, unless you configure durable storage In ephemeral containers, mount or externalize session storage; store the session ID with your business record and resume by it Claude Managed Agents Server-side event history Reconnect by listing past events; deduplicate by event ID Claude Code headless Session files on the runner Capture the session ID from JSON output and resume with it Keeping a container alive for days so its local files survive is expensive and still fails on host maintenance.

docs.h: Reconnecting to a Managed Agents session
docs.x: The event stream delivers only events that happen after it opens . Two rules follow: 1. Open the stream before sending the kickoff message, or the first events can be missed. 2. On reconnect, open a new stream, list the session's past events to recover what was missed, and skip live events whose IDs the listing already returned. A session that goes idle is not necessarily finished. Check the stop reason: end_turn means the turn finished, requires_action means a tool call (often an approval) is waiting for an answer.

On the Messages API, stop_reason tells the harness why a response ended: Stop reason State to record Next action end_turn Turn complete Check task completion against your own criteria tool_use Tool call pending Run the tool, return the result max_tokens Truncated Raise the budget or continue pause_turn Server tool paused a long turn Send the content back as the assistant turn, same tools refusal Declined Safety path, not retry Treating any text as completion, or parsing the output for a magic word, produces runs that look finished when they are not.

A run that crashed after paying but before confirming must not pay again. Combine a step journal (skip steps already done) with an idempotency key derived from the business action (the shipment, the refund), so even a repeated call returns the original result. Reordering steps only moves the crash window.

If a workflow engine orchestrates the agent, model calls must run as activities whose results are recorded. Replay re-executes deterministic workflow code and reuses recorded results; a model call made directly in workflow code runs again on replay and can produce a different decision.

Multi-day runs may outlive a snapshot. Store findings, decisions and open items as structured artifacts that any model can read, so the new snapshot resumes from facts instead of re-reading another model's long transcript. Pinning a retiring snapshot past its retirement date fails hard; restarting from scratch wastes days of valid work. Claude Code checkpoints track changes made through its file-editing tools. Files changed by shell commands or external processes are not restored by rewind, so long sessions that run scripts still need commits at safe points.

Durability items describe a run that was interrupted, resumed badly, duplicated a side effect, or misread its own state. Ask what durable record was missing (progress, session ID, event IDs, step journal, stop-reason state) and choose the option that creates it. Distractors keep infrastructure alive longer, add prompt reminders, serialize everything more often, or restart from the beginning.

docs.h: Apply it: Make Riverbend's migration agent resumable
docs.x: Riverbend's platform team runs a long Claude Code job, headless in CI, that upgrades 300 services to a new HTTP client library over two days. It runs in batches; a runner can be preempted at any time. Last month a preempted run restarted from the first service and opened duplicate pull requests for 40 services. 1. Design the durable state the job keeps, and where it lives. 2. Define how a new run resumes, including how it finds the right Claude Code session. 3. Make pull-request creation safe to repeat. Done when: a restarted run cannot open a second pull request for a service. 4. Map the run's possible endings to states an operator sees. 1. State. A migration-status.json file in a dedicated branch (or an external store), one entry per service: pending , in_progress (with session ID and branch name), pr_open (with PR number), merged or failed (with reason). The job updates it only after the step is verified (tests pass, PR created). 2. Resume. On start, the job reads the file, skips pr_open and merged , resumes in_progress entries with claude --resume <session_id> if the branch exists, and otherwise starts fresh for that service. Session IDs come from the JSON output of the earlier run. 3. Idempotent PRs. The branch name is derived from the service ( migrate/http-client/<service> ). Before creating a PR, the job checks for an open PR from that branch and records its number instead of opening another. The check is in the job's code, not in the prompt. 4. Endings. done (all entries merged or PR open), partial (turn or budget limit reached; resumable), needs_human (a service failed twice, with its reason), and error (job crashed; resumable). Each ending posts a summary to the platform channel. - Progress is stored outside the conversation and read on start. - The session ID and branch are recorded per item. - Repeating a step cannot create a duplicate side effect. - Every way the run can stop maps to a visible, actionable state.

Architecture Selection at Scale. Use production cost, reliability and quality data to decide where a running system should be a workflow and where an agent, pick the harness that gives the control a workload needs, and set reusable-pattern standards that cut duplication without hiding prompts.

At the Professional level, the architecture question is rarely "what should we build?" It is "the system is running; given what production data shows, should it change?" The exam gives you numbers (success rates, cost per task, latency, escalations by segment) and asks for the change those numbers justify.

Production traffic is rarely uniform. A support agent may resolve 91% of tickets overall while most of them follow four fixed paths. On those paths, an agent adds variance in cost and latency for no gain; on the varied remainder, it earns its cost. What the data shows What it justifies Most traffic follows a few known paths Workflows for those paths; the agent keeps the long tail A fixed chain is accurate and predictable Keep it; do not convert it to an agent Failures are machine-detectable (schema errors) An evaluator-optimizer loop with a bounded number of corrections A router misroutes requests that need two handlers An orchestrator path for multi-intent requests A costly design wins only on one query type Route that type to it; send the rest to the cheaper design Quick questions wait on a full agent loop One call with the one or two tools they need Evolve the architecture where the data shows it fails, and only there. Uniform changes, such as converting everything, adding agents everywhere, or moving everything to a bigger model, help one segment by hurting another.

When two designs run side by side, decide on outcome measures: - Cost per successful outcome, including retries and human corrections; - Escalation or correction rate by segment; - Tail latency against the target. Tool-call counts and daily token totals measure activity, not quality, and can favor a design that is cheap per call but expensive per finished task.

docs.c: The policy check that needed a loop
docs.x: Harness Gives you Choose it when Hand-written Messages API loop Full control of every step You need custom interception, unusual tool dispatch, or minimal dependencies SDK tool runner The loop handled for you Simple tool loops with no need to step inside Agent SDK Claude Code's loop, tools, hooks and permissions inside your app Agents that need hooks, permissions and sessions in your own environment Claude Managed Agents Hosted loop, sandbox per session, event history Long runs with bash and files, a team that does not want to operate containers Claude Code headless The full CLI in a pipeline Engineering tasks in CI Two constraints override convenience: 1. Compliance eligibility. If an obligation such as a business associate agreement or zero data retention applies, use a surface and runtime covered by it. A hosted feature that is not covered is ruled out, whatever the engineering saving. 2. Platform availability. Features can reach the first-party API before cloud platforms. If a platform is mandated by a cloud agreement, design for what it supports now. A team on the tool runner needed to stop certain tool calls for a policy check, rewrite some inputs, and record a span per iteration. Putting the rules in the prompt was advisory, and checking inside the tool function ran after execution. They moved those paths to an explicit loop where each step could be intercepted.

docs.h: Production readiness of a prototype loop
docs.x: Before a prototype carries real traffic, it needs: - tracing of each model and tool call with token, cost and latency attributes; - per-request turn and token limits and bounded retries enforced in the harness; - typed error handling at the tool boundary.

When many teams build on Claude, duplication and inconsistency become the operational problem: different logging, rewritten tool wrappers, drifting copies of the same procedure. Good standards: - A supported default harness with shared tracing and error handling that new agents start from. - Shared tool and MCP definitions that teams import. - Skills for shared procedures, with an owner and a version, loaded only when a task needs them, distributed through a central registry or marketplace. Requirements for adopting any third-party framework as a standard: engineers can see and log the exact requests sent to Claude, and upgrades are pinned and pass the evaluation suite before rollout. A framework that builds prompts out of sight makes debugging and evaluation harder. "Teams can no longer write inconsistent prompts" sounds like a benefit, but in exam scenarios it is the problem.

Architecture-selection items give production evidence and a proposed change. Segment the evidence, find where the current pattern fails or overspends, and choose the narrowest change that addresses it. Check compliance and platform constraints before accepting a harness. Distractors convert everything, add agents for modularity, move to the largest model, or ban working tools without a migration plan.

docs.h: Apply it: Evolve Tidewater's assistant from its traffic data
docs.x: Tidewater's assistant, Tide, runs every request through the full agent loop with all four tools loaded. A month of traces shows: 55% of requests are single metric lookups ("what was churn last month?") answered with one query_metrics call; 30% are document questions answered with search_docs ; 15% are multi-step requests that create and share reports. p95 latency is 11 seconds against a target of 8. 1. Segment the traffic and choose a pattern for each segment. 2. Decide how requests are routed to the right pattern, and what happens when the router is unsure. 3. Choose the harness for the multi-step segment and justify it. 4. Name the two measures you will compare before and after the change. 1. Segments and patterns Segment Share Pattern Single metric lookups 55% One call with query_metrics only (augmented LLM) Document questions 30% One call with search_docs , citations on Report creation and sharing 15% The existing agent with all four tools 2. Routing. A small, fast classification step labels each request; it is evaluated on 500 labeled requests before launch. When its confidence is low, the request goes to the agent, which can handle any type at higher cost. Misroutes are sampled weekly. 3. Harness. The report segment stays on the team's Agent SDK loop, because sharing a report is a consequential action that needs a hook to check tenant permissions before share_report runs. A tool runner cannot intercept that call. 4. Measures. p95 latency per segment against the 8-second target, and cost per successful answer per segment (including retries and follow-up questions), compared over two weeks before and after. - Each segment gets the simplest pattern that serves it. - Unsure routing falls back to the capable path, not to a guess. - The harness choice follows a control the workload needs. - The comparison uses outcome measures per segment.

Context and Memory Architecture. Choose the context policy for a long-running agent from what is actually filling its window, using context editing, compaction, memory, just-in-time retrieval, tool search and programmatic tool calling, and change instructions mid-conversation without breaking the cache.

Every request sends the whole context again: system prompt, tool definitions, the message history, tool results and thinking blocks. That is why long conversations get slower and more expensive even when each user message is short, and why the window eventually runs out. The goal is not to fit everything in; it is to fit the right things in.

docs.c: Match the technique to the driver
docs.x: Before choosing a technique, find out what is filling the window. Each driver has its own remedy: What fills the window Remedy Old tool results the agent no longer uses Context editing: clear older tool results automatically, keep recent ones Old thinking blocks from earlier turns Context editing that clears stale thinking A very long conversation that must continue Compaction: summarize older turns into one block Facts that must last across separate conversations Memory tool: a directory Claude reads and writes, with a backend you implement A large document or code set loaded up front Just-in-time retrieval: tools that fetch the section needed now Hundreds of tool definitions Tool search with deferred loading, and per-role tool allowlists Hundreds of independent lookups whose results pile up Programmatic tool calling, or a batch tool that returns a compact result A stable prefix re-sent on every request Prompt caching (cost and latency, not size) Compaction rewrites everything and can lose detail; use it when the conversation itself must go on. Clearing old tool results is lighter and keeps decisions intact. Caching makes repeated content cheaper but does not make the window bigger or the tool catalog easier to choose from.

Server-side compaction summarizes older turns when the input passes a threshold, so a conversation can continue past the window. It can drop details: a formatting rule the user gave early, or a record of sections already written. Two controls protect what matters: 1. Steer the summary: say what it must keep (requirements, decisions, completed work). 2. Store durable requirements outside the conversation, in a file or memory store the agent reads after compaction. In Claude Code, add instructions after /compact to shape the summary, and use a SessionStart hook with the compact matcher to re-inject state after compaction; its plain-text output is added to the context. A PostCompact hook runs at the right time but is not the route back into the conversation.

Clearing tool results changes the prompt from that point, which invalidates the cache after it. Clearing small amounts often pays the cache-write cost repeatedly. Set a minimum amount to clear so each invalidation frees enough tokens to be worth it.

docs.h: Memory: what to keep, and for whom
docs.x: Store in memory Look up fresh Preferences, roles, ongoing projects, decisions Budgets, dates, prices, counts, anything a system of record owns Entries should carry a date and source so they can be revised. Scope memory per user or per project , and review entries before they become shared: a note one session writes ("use the staging database for tests") can silently steer every other session that reads it. Memory is also an attack surface (see lesson 7.2).

Many MCP servers expose dozens of tools. Loading 180 definitions into every request costs tokens and lowers selection accuracy. Two complementary fixes: - Tool search with deferred loading: definitions load only when a search surfaces them. - Per-role allowlists: enable only the tools each agent role needs; disable the rest of a server's tools by default. Shortening descriptions to fit more tools makes selection worse, and describing tools as text in the system prompt makes them uncallable.

Prompt caching matches an exact prefix in this order: tools, then system, then messages. Editing the system prompt or tool definitions mid-conversation invalidates everything cached after the change. When instructions must change (a customer upgrades their plan, a mode switches), append the new instruction later in the message history and leave the cached prefix untouched. Putting per-user details at the start of the system prompt makes every prefix unique, so every request writes a new cache entry. Stable content goes first; per-user and per-request content goes after the breakpoint.

docs.h: A policy for very long conversations
docs.x: For agents that run for hundreds of turns under a cost ceiling, separate what must be remembered from what can be trimmed: - record commitments and decisions as structured notes the agent reads every turn; - compact or trim older turns once the context passes a threshold; - never drop turns blindly or ask users to repeat themselves.

Context items describe a long-running agent near its limit or its budget, often with a token breakdown. Identify the largest driver and pick the technique built for it; check whether the proposed change breaks the cache or loses something the agent still needs. Distractors raise max_tokens (an output limit), buy a bigger window, cache everything, compact every turn, or edit the system prompt dynamically.

docs.h: Apply it: Set the context policy for Cobalt's triage agent
docs.x: Cobalt's triage agent handles some long threads: a patient with a chronic condition may exchange 200 messages with the care team over weeks, in one conversation. The token breakdown for long threads is: 52% old search_protocols results, 18% lookup_patient and get_care_plan results repeated on many turns, 12% thinking from earlier turns, 10% system prompt and tools (cached), 8% conversation text. The privacy officer will not allow patient content in any store the team has not approved. 1. Assign a technique to each driver in the breakdown. 2. Decide what must never be lost when old turns are trimmed, and where it lives. 3. Check your policy against the cache, and adjust it if needed. 4. Say what you would not use, and why. 1. Techniques Driver Technique Old protocol search results (52%) Context editing: clear tool results older than the last few, with a minimum clear amount Repeated patient and care-plan results (18%) Fetch fresh when needed; keep only a compact current summary in the conversation Old thinking (12%) Context editing that clears thinking blocks from earlier turns System prompt and tools (10%) Already cached; keep the prefix stable 2. Must not be lost. Commitments made to the patient ("nurse will call Tuesday"), allergies flagged, and open follow-ups. They are written to a structured care-thread note in Cobalt's approved clinical record store (not a new memory store), and the agent reads it every turn. 3. Cache. Clearing invalidates the cache after the cleared point only, and the system prompt and tools stay cached. Setting a minimum clear amount (for example 30,000 tokens) avoids paying cache writes every few turns. 4. Not used. Compaction on every turn (lossy and costly for clinical commitments), a bigger window (cost grows with every turn), and a new memory store for patient facts (not approved by the privacy officer). - Each technique targets a measured driver. - Facts that must survive trimming live outside the conversation, in an approved store. - The policy keeps the cached prefix stable and batches clearing. - Rejected options have a stated reason.

Reliability Engineering for Claude Services. Classify each failure a Claude integration sees (rate limit, overload, invalid request, length stop, context-window stop, refusal) and give it its own response, then add circuit breakers, retry budgets, graceful degradation and tested fallbacks across models, regions and platforms.

The most common reliability bug in Claude integrations is a single retry path for every failure. Different outcomes need different responses, and treating them alike multiplies cost, repeats refusals and turns outages into retry storms. Classify first, then respond.

Outcome What it means Correct response 429 rate_limit_error Your requests exceed a limit Wait at least retry-after , back off with jitter, retry on the same model 529 overloaded_error , brief 500s Transient capacity or server problem A few retries with backoff; then a tested fallback Overload lasting many minutes Sustained capacity problem Circuit breaker plus fallback routing 400 invalid_request_error , 413 too large The request itself is wrong Never retry as is; fix or shrink it, alert 401, 403 Credentials or permissions Fix credentials; retries will not help stop_reason: max_tokens Output hit its budget Raise the budget, ask for less, or continue from the partial response stop_reason: model_context_window_exceeded Input outgrew the window Compact or clear, then resend stop_reason: refusal The model declined Safety path: safe message, log, review; never route around it Rate limits are waited out. Length stops are fixed by changing the budget or the output. Refusals go to a safety path. A retry path that cannot tell them apart is the root cause, not the retry count.

- Honor retry-after and add jitter so many clients do not retry in step. - Retry at one layer only. Retries in the client, the agent loop and the gateway multiply into each other. - Use a retry budget: cap retries as a share of total requests across the service, so a partial outage cannot multiply load. - Never retry a side effect without an idempotency key (see lesson 1.2).

When a dependency is failing, immediate retries from every instance create a storm that delays recovery and can trigger rate limits after capacity returns. A circuit breaker opens after repeated failures (calls fail fast), probes with a few requests after a cooldown, and closes when they succeed. Use one per dependency: the Claude API, and each tool backend. At the tool boundary, an open breaker returns an error result immediately ("shipping system unavailable, retry later"), so the agent can tell the user and continue with what still works instead of waiting 30 seconds per call.

Keep the core function available with reduced capability: - show the decision with standard reason codes when an explanation cannot be generated; - queue non-urgent work and finish it when the service recovers; - decouple a page with a strict availability target from a slower analysis step with a durable queue, an "analysis pending" state and a dead-letter queue. Error pages, invented answers and users waiting on ten-minute retries are not graceful.

docs.c: The beta header that broke failover
docs.x: Fallback Must be true before relying on it Cross-model The fallback model passes the task's quality floor on the evaluation set Cross-region The region supports the same model and the features your requests use Cross-platform (first-party API, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry) A separate request configuration that uses only features that platform supports Every fallback response should be logged with its model and path, with an alert when the fallback share passes a threshold. An untested fallback turns an availability incident into a quality incident. Refusals are never part of the availability chain: retrying a refused request on another model can route around a legitimate safety decision. A team's fallback to Vertex AI failed with request errors because its requests carried a beta header for a tool Vertex AI did not support yet. The fix was a platform-specific configuration, tested regularly, not removing the feature from the primary path.

Long non-streaming requests can exceed client or network idle timeouts. Stream long generations. With streaming, an error can arrive mid-stream after some text was shown: detect it, mark the partial output as incomplete, retry, and replace the partial output rather than appending to it.
Reliability includes reporting what really happened. If Claude's call succeeded but the tool's side effect failed, the agent must report the failure, not success.

Reliability items show a mix of failures in traces and a proposed policy. Classify each outcome, then pick the option that gives each class its correct response, bounds retry load, and uses only tested fallbacks. Distractors increase retries for everything, switch traffic permanently, remove the fallback, retry 400s, rotate keys to dodge limits, or treat refusals as transient.

docs.x: Cobalt's visit-summary service calls Claude once per visit transcript, with outputs up to 6,000 tokens. Last quarter, during a provider capacity incident, it retried every failure immediately and was rate-limited for 40 minutes after recovery. Scale and Throughput Management. Work out which constraint binds a high-volume Claude workload (requests, input tokens, output tokens, or batch economics), then apply the matching lever, from caching and routing to queues with backpressure, batch processing, workspace limits and per-tenant quotas.

Throughput problems look alike from the outside (429 errors, growing queues, slow responses) but have different causes. The exam gives you the numbers and expects you to do the arithmetic before choosing a fix.

docs.c: The template that was not cached · Do the arithmetic first
docs.x: Rate limits are measured per model in requests per minute , input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute . Compute each against its limit: 90 requests a minute, each with 40,000 input tokens and 600 output tokens. Limits: 4,000 requests, 2,000,000 input tokens and 400,000 output tokens per minute.  - Requests: 90 against 4,000, fine. - Input: 3,600,000 against 2,000,000, over . - Output: 54,000 against 400,000, fine.  35,000 of each request's tokens are the same contract template. For most current models, only uncached input tokens count toward the input-token limit, so caching the template brings uncached input to about 450,000 a minute. Binding constraint Levers Input tokens per minute Cache stable prefixes; trim context per request; route high-volume steps to another model Output tokens per minute Right-size outputs; move long generation to batch Requests per minute Combine independent calls; queue and smooth bursts Cost per token on offline work Message Batches API Latency requirement Real-time requests, even when batch would be cheaper Multiply rate by size for each limit before choosing a fix. Flat request counts with growing tokens per request point at token throughput, and the remedy is less input per request, not fewer requests.

Limits are enforced continuously, and a jump from near zero to thousands of requests within seconds can be limited even below the per-minute ceiling. Ramp new traffic gradually and honor retry-after while doing so.

A queue absorbs bursts and lets workers send at a steady rate within the limits. When demand stays above capacity, an unbounded queue only converts load into latency until the work is useless. Backpressure means: - a bounded queue; - rejecting or deferring new work when it is full, so producers slow down; - expiring items older than their usefulness; - priority for work with a user waiting over background work. Adding workers does not create rate-limit capacity.

The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously and costs less per token, with results returned when each batch completes (often well within an hour, but not guaranteed to be fast). It fits catalog generation, nightly re-scoring, large evaluation runs and backfills. It does not fit work with a freshness target of minutes. Each result carries its own outcome: an ended batch can still contain errored or expired requests, which the pipeline must resubmit or report.

Mechanism What it isolates Workspaces with their own rate and spend limits Workloads within the organization (production chat versus experiments) Per-tenant quotas at your gateway (token buckets for requests and tokens) Customers of a multi-tenant product Fair scheduling across tenants One tenant's burst from everyone else's latency Metering against plan allowances before the call Plan caps, enforced before shared capacity is used API keys within one workspace share its limits, so one key per tenant does not isolate tenants. Monthly invoices and daily resets do not enforce anything during the day.

Forecast demand in the units limits use, and model tokens per unit of work , not just users: - sessions times tokens per session (input uncached, input cached, output) per product line; - planned feature launches and their effect on tokens per session (a new agent feature can multiply them); - peak-to-average ratios and holiday multipliers. For a peak above current capacity, reduce what each request consumes on the constrained model (caching, trimming) and move high-volume, simple steps to a smaller model with separate limits.

Throughput items give rates, sizes and limits. Compute each constraint, identify the one that binds, and pick the lever for it. Check whether the workload can wait (batch) or needs isolation (workspaces, gateway quotas). Distractors add workers, rotate keys, retry harder, rebuild the index twice as often, or choose by cost when latency is the requirement.

Production MCP and Change Management. Run MCP servers, model versions and prompts as production changes, with authenticated remote servers, backward-compatible tool schemas and deprecation, pinned snapshots tested against behavior changes, configuration parity across platforms and gateways, versioned prompts, and staged rollouts with rollback.

In a Claude system, behavior changes come from more places than code: an MCP server's tool definitions, the model snapshot, the system prompt, a gateway between clients and the API, and the configuration for each platform. Each needs the discipline of a production release: versioning, testing, staged rollout, a rollback path and a record of what was live when.

A remote MCP server is a shared service that many agents call. Its security posture follows the MCP authorization and security guidance: - Authenticate clients with OAuth and validate that each token was issued for this server (its audience). - Never pass the client's token through to downstream APIs. The server obtains its own credentials, scoped to what its tools need. Token passthrough breaks audience checks and creates confused-deputy risks. - Authorize per user when the server acts for users, rather than one powerful service credential for every request. When an agent uses a third-party server, expose only what it needs. With the Messages API MCP connector, disable the server's tools by default and enable the required ones, and give the server a token scoped to the same access.

Change Effect on callers Practice Add an optional parameter with a default None Ship it Add a required parameter Breaks every caller Make it optional, or publish a new tool version Change the output format Breaks callers that parse it New version beside the old one Remove a tool Breaks its callers Deprecate with a dated plan Deprecation needs usage data (who still calls the old version), warnings the callers will see (a notice in the tool's result), a dated removal plan , and escalation when owners do not respond. Changing a format in place, or forcing everyone to update on the same day, causes incidents. Dependencies that change independently, such as a vendor's MCP server, need their versions recorded with each trace and pinned where possible, so a behavior change can be matched to a dependency change in minutes.

docs.c: The canary that caught a cost regression
docs.x: Pin production to a dated snapshot ID . An alias points at the newest snapshot and can change behavior without a deploy. Treat each model change as a release: 1. Read the migration guide's behavior changes, such as more literal instruction following or parameters that are no longer supported. 2. Refresh the evaluation suite with recent production cases, including failures; a suite every model passes cannot show a difference. 3. Compare results by category and field by field, including output format, not only the pass rate. 4. Review prompts for implicit expectations the new model may follow more literally. 5. Canary on a small share of traffic, watching quality, length and cost, then widen. 6. Finish before the retirement date. A new snapshot on 5% of traffic left task success unchanged but made outputs 45% longer and conversations 30% more expensive. The team paused, adjusted prompts for length, and re-ran the canary before widening.

Keep prompts in version control with IDs, and log the prompt version on every trace. Then any response can be traced to the prompt that produced it, and rollback is a configuration change. Progressive rollout for prompts: - release to a small share first, widening in stages while quality and error metrics hold; - define rollback triggers in advance and keep the previous version ready; - keep online monitoring on even when offline evaluation passed.

When the same agent runs on the first-party API and on Bedrock, Vertex AI or Foundry, configuration drifts unless it is generated from one versioned source with per-platform settings (model identifiers, supported features) and a parity check. Run the evaluation suite on each platform before promotion. An LLM gateway is the right place for cross-cutting controls: central credential management, per-application quotas, consistent logging. It must forward what the API needs, including version and beta headers; a gateway upgrade that strips them breaks features that still work when called directly. It is the wrong place for silently rewriting prompts, overriding the model an application asked for, or requiring approval of every prompt change. Shipping a model change together with a new tool that depends on it makes rollback partial: reverting the model breaks the tool's route. Ship changes so they can be rolled back separately, or roll them back as a unit.

Change-management items describe a change that broke something, or a change about to ship. Look for the missing discipline: backward compatibility, a version record, a pinned snapshot, a refreshed evaluation, a staged rollout, a parity check, or a gateway that alters requests. Distractors announce changes in chat, restart everything, rely on aliases, freeze prompts forever, or cut over on the deadline.

Retrieval and Knowledge Grounding at Scale. Choose between agentic search and RAG for a production corpus, tune chunking, embeddings, hybrid search and reranking from stage-level measurements, and design grounding (citations, declared uncertainty, calibrated confidence, permission-aware retrieval) so answers can be checked.

A grounded answer can fail at four stages: the evidence was not in the index (data), was not retrieved (recall), was retrieved but ranked too low to reach the model (ranking), or reached the model and was not used correctly (generation). Fixing the wrong stage wastes effort. Diagnose by stage first.

For a sample of wrong answers, check where the right passage was lost: Finding Stage Typical fixes The document is missing or outdated in the index Data Incremental indexing with deletions; version and date metadata The right passage is not in the candidate set Recall Better chunking, contextual embeddings, hybrid search, metadata filters It is in the top 50 but not the top 5 Ranking A reranker; choose cutoffs from measured recall It reached the model, which used another passage Generation Instructions, quote-first answering, citations 140 had the right passage outside the top 50 (recall), 40 had it below the cutoff (ranking), 20 had it in context (generation). Prompt changes would have addressed 10% of the problem; recall work addressed 70%. Measure stages separately: recall at k isolates retrieval, and groundedness (are the answer's claims supported by the passages provided?) isolates generation.

Favors agentic search (list, grep, open, query) Favors RAG (index, retrieve, rerank) Content changes many times a day (code, live records) Large, slowly changing corpus Answers follow references across files or records One retrieval step answers most questions Freshness matters more than speed Tight latency targets Agentic search usually costs more tokens and time per question; it buys freshness and multi-hop reasoning.

- Structure-aware chunking keeps tables whole with their headings and respects section boundaries. Fixed-size cuts split tables from their labels. - Contextual retrieval prepends a short, generated description of each chunk's place in its document before embedding, so chunks like "the limit in clause 4.2 shall not exceed this amount" become retrievable and interpretable. - Embedding model changes require re-embedding the whole corpus, ideally into a new index switched over after evaluation; vectors from different models are not comparable.

Dense embeddings blur exact tokens such as part numbers and codes. Hybrid search adds keyword matching (for example BM25) and merges the lists. Metadata filters (product, tenant, version, access rights) remove wrong-scope content before ranking. A reranker reorders a larger candidate set so the best passages reach the model; tune how many candidates it scores from recall curves, since scoring hundreds per query costs latency.

Practice How Source citation Send documents with citations enabled, or pass retrieved passages as search result blocks, so claims link to exact text Uncertainty declaration Instruct Claude to say when the sources do not cover the question, rather than answering from memory A no-evidence path When nothing passes a relevance threshold, a designed response and a route to a person Confidence signals Derive from evidence (how many passages support the answer, whether they agree), then calibrate against reviewed answers Source policy Apply the same allowed sources to every retrieval path; a second, unrestricted search tool bypasses the policy The share of answers with a citation can rise while grounding gets worse: citing anything is not citing correctly. Measure whether each cited passage supports its claim.
Filter results by what the user may see before they reach the model. Once a confidential memo is in the context, no instruction can un-retrieve it, and ranking tweaks do not enforce access.

Retrieval items give stage-level evidence or a symptom (wrong product, exact codes failing, tables failing, stale policies, citations that do not support claims). Locate the stage, then choose the fix for that stage. Distractors change the prompt for a recall problem, retrieve far more passages, enlarge chunks blindly, drop a stage that drives quality, or answer from training data.

Telemetry and Instrumentation. Instrument agent loops with distributed traces, record complete token, cost and cache metrics, make grounding and reasoning traceable, emit structured events with a shared schema, and capture content only where privacy rules allow it.

An agent request is a tree: model calls, tool calls, retries and subagents. One log line per request with the total latency and the final answer cannot explain a 50-second request or a wrong answer. Instrumentation for Claude systems has to show the tree, count every token category, and do it without storing content that privacy rules forbid.

Span Key attributes Request (root) Request and trace IDs, tenant or user ID (pseudonymous), route, prompt version, model snapshot Model call Model, input, output, cache-read and cache-creation tokens, stop reason, latency, time to first token Tool call Tool name, server and version, duration, error flag and error category, result size Retry Attempt number, error type, backoff Subagent Parent span, its own model and tool spans Propagate the trace context into subagents and tool services; without it, their work shows up as orphaned traces that cannot be joined to the request. Errors should be recorded as structured types (rate limit, overloaded, invalid request), not just success or failure, so dashboards can separate them.

With caching on, input_tokens excludes the cached prefix. True input is: input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens each priced at its own rate (cache reads cheaper, cache writes dearer than normal input). A cost metric built from input and output tokens alone under-reports spend once caching is on. For attribution, tag every request with tenant and feature identifiers at the gateway and record them on its usage event.

Signal Likely cause Cache reads near zero, creation near zero Prefix below the model's minimum cacheable length (no error is raised) Creation high on nearly every request Something before the breakpoint changes per request: a timestamp, a user ID, tool order Creation spikes at intervals Entries expiring between requests; consider the longer lifetime Read share falls after a release The release changed or reordered the prefix Track cache-read tokens as a share of total input and cache-creation tokens over time per route.

To classify a wrong answer, the trace must show what evidence the model had: retrieved passage IDs and versions, retrieval scores, and the citations used. For reasoning, request summarized thinking where the model hides thinking text by default, and store it under the same content policy as other captured content.

Never log API keys, and avoid free-text fields that each team writes differently.

Zero data retention concerns what the provider retains; your own observability is your responsibility. Where policy forbids storing message content: - capture metadata (tokens, latency, stop reasons, tool names, error codes, versions) with content capture off by default ; - where debugging content is allowed, enable it per conversation with recorded consent, redact identifiers before storage, and keep it for the shortest period allowed, under a retention policy separate from metrics. Claude Code can export OpenTelemetry metrics and events to an organization's collector, configured centrally through managed settings; it includes prompt text only when that is explicitly enabled. Turning off all telemetry is the wrong reading. Metadata about requests is your own operational data and is what makes the system debuggable.

Production Monitoring and Alerting. Define SLIs and SLOs that cover how LLM services really fail (slow starts, poor answers, refusals), alert on error-budget burn, build dashboards for each audience, and detect quality drift, behavioral regressions and anomalous usage, especially after model updates.

An LLM service can return HTTP 200 on every request and still be failing: answers start too slowly, are wrong, ignore a required format, or refuse legitimate requests. Monitoring must measure those failures directly, alert on what threatens the objectives, and notice when behavior shifts after a change.

SLI What it catches Availability: share of requests that complete without error Outages and error spikes Time to first token at p95 (streamed) Slow starts users notice Total latency at p95 Long tails on agent tasks Quality: pass rate of a sampled, rubric-based evaluation of live answers Wrong or poor answers returning 200 Refusal rate per route Over-blocking after prompt or document changes Truncation rate ( max_tokens stops) Budgets too small for real inputs A quality SLO is only usable when its SLI is measurable. "95% of answers are correct" needs a stated sampling and scoring method, or it is never evaluated.

docs.h: Alert on burn, not on blips
docs.x: Paging whenever more than 1% of requests fail in one minute produces dozens of pages a week for blips. Burn-rate alerts measure how fast the error budget is being used and combine a short and a long window: page when both show fast burn, ticket when the slow window shows a steady burn. When an SLO is being missed, the error budget decides whether reliability work takes priority, and diagnosis starts by locating the tail: which stage and which cohorts make the slow requests. Changing the target or the statistic only hides the problem.

Audience Shows On-call Errors by source (model API by type, each tool, application code); p95 latency by stage; current SLO burn Engineering Tokens by category, cache-read share, tool-call rates, stop reasons, by model and prompt version Executives Cost per successful outcome by product; SLO attainment Finance Spend by tenant and feature; projected month-end spend

docs.c: A doubling hidden by a flat outcome
docs.x: Model updates and prompt changes can change behavior without changing error rates. Watch output properties , segmented by model and prompt version: - answer length, presence of required sections, format validity; - tool-call rates per tool, especially consequential tools (refunds, emails); - refusal and truncation rates; - sampled quality and groundedness scores. After a snapshot update, resolution rate stayed flat while the share of conversations calling the refund tool rose from 4% to 9%. Only a per-tool rate, compared across versions, showed it. For noisy metrics, use control bands from a rolling baseline (mean and standard deviation) to catch spikes, and run rules (for example, several consecutive readings beyond the mean) to catch slow drift that never crosses an extreme band. Compare like with like: the same day last week or the same segment, so weekly patterns and traffic mix do not cause false alarms.

Compare each API key and tenant with its own baseline. A jump from 2 million to 60 million tokens a day from one key, with near-identical prompts at all hours, may be a leaked credential or a runaway job; route it to an owner for review. Organization-wide totals hide individual spikes, and automatic permanent blocks punish legitimate growth. A rising refusal rate can mean the assistant is blocking legitimate requests. It belongs on the quality dashboard with an owner, not in the security team's queue by default.

Monitoring items describe what a team watches and something it missed or was paged for needlessly. Choose the SLI, alert or dashboard change that would have caught the real failure or stopped the noise. Distractors raise thresholds, average away the tail, suppress alerts by day, rely on user complaints, or monitor only an outcome metric that stayed flat.

Trace Analysis at Scale. Keep the traces that matter with tail-based sampling, aggregate by cohort to find systemic failures no single trace shows, label failures at scale with validated model-assisted classification, and avoid the statistical traps of mixed cohorts and confounded comparisons.

At millions of traces a day, reading traces one at a time finds anecdotes, not causes. Systemic issues, such as a tool that fails for one tenant's data format or a prompt that hurts one language, look ordinary in each trace and only appear when traces are grouped. Trace analysis at scale is about keeping the right traces, grouping them the right way, and drawing honest conclusions.

Strategy Decides Keeps rare failures? Head-based random sampling Before the request runs No: a 1% sample of a 0.05% failure keeps a handful Tail-based sampling After the trace completes Yes: keep every error, slow or unusual trace, sample routine successes Stratified review sampling By segment Covers every route, tenant tier and outcome Anomaly over-sampling By unusual features Surfaces new failure modes first Keep all error traces even when successes are sampled heavily: errors are rare and carry the most diagnostic value. Successful traces still matter as the comparison group.

When an overall rate moves and no single trace looks wrong: 1. Group failures by cohort: document type, language, tenant, route, tool, model snapshot, prompt version, MCP server version. 2. Compare failure rates across cohorts to see where the change is concentrated. 3. Contrast failing and passing traces in the affected cohort on attributes such as tools called, stop reasons and result sizes, to find the mechanism. 4. Line up the change timeline: a jump at 14:05 next to a deployment or configuration change at 14:04 is a strong lead. Question Aggregation Why did cost per task rise 25%? Tokens per task by category (input, output, cached reads, tool results), and turns per task by task type Which change broke things at 14:05? Error rate split by each version attribute Why do failures look like "nothing found"? Failures by tool, tenant and result type

Claude can label thousands of failed conversations against a defined category list . The labels need checking against a human-reviewed sample before they drive decisions. The same applies to estimating properties such as groundedness over 50,000 reports a month: score a sample with a judge that checks each claim against its sources, and validate the judge against human review first.

Complex Failure Diagnosis. Isolate where a complex failure began (model output, agent harness, tools or data) using replay, request diffs, repeated trials and agent-boundary comparisons, and treat refusals and grounding failures as failure classes with causes of their own.

When an agent gives a wrong answer, the instinct is to blame the model and change the prompt or the model. In production, many failures begin elsewhere: a harness that truncated history, a tool wrapper that turned a timeout into an empty list, a stale index, a handoff that cut off a specialist's findings, or a renderer that broke a correct table. The skill is to find the first wrong step and the layer it belongs to before changing anything.

Origin Typical evidence Model output The exact recorded request, replayed, reproduces the wrong answer Agent harness The request the model received differs from what it should have: truncated history, missing system prompt, mismatched tool_use IDs, cut-off handoffs, dropped tool results Tools The tool returned something misleading: an empty list on timeout, a partial result without saying so, an unreported error Data The source is missing, stale or wrong: a document not indexed, a superseded policy, wrong-tenant records A fifth place is below or after the application: serving infrastructure, or a rendering layer that displays correct output wrongly. Correct classification decides who fixes what.

- Replay the exact recorded request (same snapshot, system prompt, messages, tool results) several times. If replays are consistently right, the model behaved correctly on that input; look at what was actually sent, or at steps after the model. - Diff the requests of differing runs. Different retrieved documents or tool results explain different outputs without any model variation. - Repeated trials on fixed inputs. An intermittent failure (one run in eight) must be measured as a rate. Change one variable at a time, holding the snapshot, tools and inputs fixed; a single successful run proves nothing. - Compare across agent boundaries. A complete output on one side and a truncated input on the other locates the failure in the handoff code. - Follow concentrated signals. A failure that clusters by turn count, language, tenant, product or stop reason points at the component tied to that dimension.

In multi-turn failures, the symptom appears late but the cause is early: a fact given in turn 3 and lost when the harness trimmed to the last 10 turns cannot be recalled in turn 14 by any model. Failures that start beyond a turn threshold suggest a context policy at that threshold (clearing that removes evidence of completed steps, for example). In multi-agent failures, trace back to the first boundary where something went wrong: a subagent that turned a failed lookup into an estimate without saying so, and a coordinator that then propagated it faithfully.

A rise in refusals has causes like any other failure. If it starts with a prompt or document change and clusters on the topic that change mentions, the new text is being read as a ban; narrow its wording. Over-refusal of legitimate requests is a quality failure, not a security success.

Locate the stage: missing or stale data, retrieval recall, ranking, or generation (see lesson 2.4). Check whether the documents exist and are current, then whether the right passage reached the model, before rewriting prompts or switching models.

docs.c: "I couldn't find your order" · Infrastructure can degrade quality
docs.x: An agent that calls the same tool with the same query again and again is usually not getting what it expects: the result looks incomplete or ambiguous, or the harness drops it under load. Check the trace before raising turn limits, which only let the loop run longer. An order agent told customers their orders did not exist. Traces showed empty tool results; the tool service logs showed timeouts. The wrapper returned an empty list on timeout, so the model answered correctly from what it saw. The fix was to return an error result marked retryable. Anthropic's postmortem of three issues describes quality problems caused by serving infrastructure that affected some requests and were hard to see in evaluations. Unusual user reports, such as garbled characters across unrelated prompts, deserve investigation even when evaluations look normal.

Diagnosis items give evidence from traces, logs and replays. Ask: what did the model actually receive, and was the answer reasonable given that? Pick the conclusion the evidence supports and the fix at that layer. Distractors blame the model by reflex, switch models, add prompt instructions, raise limits, retry, or close the report after one good run.

docs.h: Apply it: Diagnose Cobalt's declined messages
docs.x: After a protocol update added a paragraph about protecting mental-health information, Cobalt's triage agent declined to classify 4% of messages about anxiety medication. At the same time, a few urgent messages took over 15 minutes to reach a nurse. The team has traces with stop reasons, tool spans and prompt versions, and can replay recorded requests. 1. Form a hypothesis for each symptom and say which layer it points to. 2. Design the test that confirms or rules out each hypothesis. 3. Propose the fix for the refusals, and how you will know it worked. 4. Say what you will not do, and why. 1. Hypotheses. Refusals: the new paragraph is being read as a ban on discussing mental-health medication (model output responding to a prompt change). Slow urgent messages: a harness or tool issue, for example the search_protocols call timing out and retrying, or the approval queue not prioritizing urgent items (harness or workflow). 2. Tests. Refusals: replay 100 refused requests with the previous prompt version and with the new one, three trials each, everything else fixed; compare refusal rates. Slow messages: read the spans of every urgent message over 15 minutes, grouped by stage (model calls, each tool, nurse queue wait), and compare with fast urgent messages. 3. Fix. Reword the paragraph to say what is restricted (sharing mental-health details outside the care team) and that classifying and drafting replies for the care team is expected. Success: refusal rate on the replay set back to baseline, and the live refusal rate per route back within its band for a week, with no rise in policy-violation findings. 4. Not doing. Switching models (the change began with the prompt), retrying refused messages on another model (routes around a safety decision), and adding keyword filters (would block legitimate questions). - Each symptom has a hypothesis tied to a layer. - Tests hold everything fixed except the suspected factor, with repeated trials. - The fix has a measurable success criterion. - Reflexive model changes and retries are ruled out with reasons.

Incident Response and Learning Loops. Lead an LLM-system incident from triage to mitigation, rollback and communication, including quality regressions with no errors, and turn every incident into regression evaluations, monitoring coverage and blameless postmortem actions.

LLM systems have the usual incidents (outages, dependency failures, capacity problems) and some of their own: quality regressions with no errors , after a prompt, model, index or tool change. The response pattern is the same: triage, mitigate first, communicate, then learn. What differs is that the most likely causes are changes to non-code components, and the most valuable learning output is a new evaluation case.

- Is it real, and how bad? Impact (users, money, safety), scope (which routes, tenants, categories) and trend. - What changed? Deployments, prompt and model versions, index rebuilds, MCP server versions, provider status. The trace version attributes and change log answer this quickly. - Who leads? An incident commander coordinates; responders investigate; one person communicates.

Mitigation does not need the root cause. Situation Mitigation A recent release correlates with the regression and a tested rollback exists Roll back now, then diagnose and fix forward One category behaves wrongly, cause unknown A feature flag that stops that behavior (for example, route that claim category to adjusters) A dependency is degraded for days Circuit breaker, honest degraded messaging, keep the rest working A bad retrieval index Roll back to a known-good index with a small freshness gap Provider capacity incident Bounded retries, tested fallback, queued non-urgent work Waiting for the engineer's fix while customers see wrong interest rates, adding a warning banner, or shutting down working features are worse trade-offs. If a model change and a dependent tool shipped together, rolling back one breaks the other. Release changes so they can be rolled back separately, or as a unit.

Post the impact, what users can do, and when the next update will come, then keep to that cadence. Waiting for the root cause, or describing a provider incident as "maintenance", erodes trust. Record a timestamped timeline as you go , from change events, alerts and actions, rather than reconstructing it from memory a week later.

An agent in the on-call channel can read alerts, dashboards and recent deploys and post a diagnosis within minutes. Consequential actions, such as a rollback, wait for the on-call engineer's approval, and everything it finds and does is recorded in the incident thread. In tiered automation, the highest tier may run only pre-approved runbooks and must hand its findings to humans; it never merges code changes directly.

A fix stops new damage; it does not correct the 3,000 customers who already received a misleading message or the claims already approved. Identify affected records from logs and correct them. When a provider announces a quality issue that affected your window, use your own traces to find the affected requests.

Output Example Regression evaluation The incident's cases (multi-currency quotes, medication dosages) added to the release gate Monitoring coverage The signal that would have caught it sooner (refusal rate per route) with an alert and an owner; check similar signals for the same gap Runbook update Triggers for quality incidents, and rollback steps for prompts, models and indexes Contributing factors System conditions: an evaluation coverage gap, a release to all traffic at once Postmortems are blameless : people describe what happened candidly when they are not blamed, which exposes the conditions that allowed the failure. Action items are specific, owned and enforced by the system. "Be more careful" is not an action item.

Incident items put you mid-incident or in the postmortem. Choose the action that contains harm fastest without waiting for root cause, communicates clearly, or converts the incident into durable protection. Distractors wait, freeze all releases, blame individuals, roll back everything, delete evidence, or treat a deployed fix as the end of the work.

Evaluation System Design. Build offline evaluation that gates releases, from golden sets, regression suites and behavioral checks to stable CI gates and release criteria for prompt, model and agent changes, and keep the suite valid against contamination, saturation and coverage gaps.

An evaluation suite is the release gate for everything that changes a Claude system's behavior: prompts, models, tools, retrieval, and agent configuration such as CLAUDE.md, Skills and hooks. A gate is only useful if it detects real regressions, ignores noise, and stays representative of production as both the system and the traffic change.

Component Purpose Golden set Real inputs from the target workload with accepted outputs; start with 20 to 50 and grow Regression cases Every production incident becomes a case, kept permanently Edge and adversarial cases Hard inputs, unusual formats, languages, policy boundaries Behavioral checks Verify outcomes and side effects: the query returns the right data, the agent did not modify a read-only table, no sensitive field reached the logs Behavioral checks test what the output does , not how it is worded. Keyword checks and exact string matches are weak proxies that fail correct answers and pass wrong ones.

Task Metrics Extraction Field-level accuracy against verified values; schema validity Retrieval-grounded answers Retrieval recall and precision; groundedness (claims supported by provided passages) Agentic tasks Task success by outcome checks; side effects within scope; cost and turns Generation Rubric-based scores from calibrated judges (lesson 5.2) Fluency can rise while groundedness falls, so a fluency score cannot stand in for grounding.

docs.h: Gates that are stable and sensitive
docs.x: - Repeated trials: agent outputs vary between runs. Run each case several times and gate on pass rates; when a gate's verdict changes on rerun, it is measuring noise. Engineers rerunning until green is a sign the gate needs trials, not removal. - Per-category results: gate on each category's floor, not only the overall score, so a regression in refunds cannot hide behind an improvement elsewhere. - Paired comparison: compare versions on the same cases with repeated trials and check whether the difference exceeds the observed variance before calling 89% better than 87%. - Isolation of the checks: an agent under evaluation must not be able to change what grades it. Run checks from a copy made before the agent runs, and fail any run that changes files outside its allowed paths.

For a model or prompt change: no category below its quality floor , and cost and latency within stated budgets . An overall gain can hide a category regression; a cheaper price per token can still cost more if outputs grow. Run the suite on every change to anything that steers the agent, including CLAUDE.md, Skills and hooks, not only code. A trimmed CLAUDE.md that drops a logging rule can pass code review and fail a behavioral check.

docs.c: Labels from the model under test
docs.x: Threat Sign Remedy Saturation Every release scores 98 to 100% while production escalations rise Add recent production failures and harder cases Contamination Cases copied from public sources may be in training data Use private, production-derived cases Coverage gaps 30% of traffic is Spanish and Portuguese, the suite is English only Cases sampled from real traffic in each segment, results reported per segment Stale labels Requirements changed, golden answers did not An owner per golden set, reviews on requirement changes, versioned sets Regenerating golden answers with the current model each quarter grades the model against itself. Deleting cases whenever a release fails them removes the regressions the suite exists to catch.

Evaluation-design items describe a suite or gate and a symptom: flaky verdicts, a regression that passed, saturated scores, a suite that misses a language, an agent that gamed its checks. Choose the change that makes the gate measure the real property reliably. Distractors raise thresholds on saturated suites, remove gates, allow unlimited reruns, check keywords, or let the model write its own labels.

LLM-as-Judge Engineering. Treat an LLM judge as a measurement instrument, with a rubric clear enough for humans to agree on, agreement with human labels measured by category and corrected for chance, known biases controlled, and recalibration whenever the judge's model changes.

An LLM judge scales evaluation to thousands of outputs, but its verdicts mean something only if they agree with careful human judgment. A judge that has never been checked against human labels is an opinion, and gating releases on it can make quality worse while every release passes.

1. Write a rubric with specific, observable criteria and anchored examples of each score. 2. Check that humans agree with each other using the rubric. If two raters disagree on 40% of items, fix the rubric first; a judge cannot be calibrated to labels that disagree. 3. Measure judge agreement with human labels using chance-corrected statistics (such as Cohen's kappa), by category as well as overall. 4. Give gating authority only where agreement is acceptable. Elsewhere, keep humans in the loop or improve the rubric. A judge agreed with humans 92% of the time overall, but 55% on refund-policy exceptions. It could gate routine cases, not exceptions, until its rubric for exceptions improved.

Bias Sign Control Position In pairwise comparison, picks the first (or second) response more often than humans do Randomize order, or run both orders and count a win only when both agree Verbosity Scores longer answers higher at equal quality Rubric criteria that give no credit for length; re-measure on labeled pairs Self-preference Rates outputs from its own model family higher than humans do Measure agreement per source model; use a judge from a different family for those comparisons Missing reference Grades factual accuracy without the source document Give the judge the reference material Truncating answers to equal length removes content the judge needs; using a larger judge does not guarantee the biases disappear.

Broad numeric scales (1 to 10) tend to cluster and drift, and a 0.2-point change is hard to interpret. Prefer pass or fail checks on defined criteria , each with a short reason. Reasons make verdicts auditable: spot-check them against human review to find judge errors. For pairwise verdicts run in both orders, inconsistent pairs are ties, and the rate of inconsistency is itself a calibration signal for position bias.

- Judge drift across model versions: moving the judge to a new snapshot changes what its scores mean. Re-run calibration on the human-labeled set and reset thresholds before it gates again. - Optimizing against the judge: if the pass rate rises steadily while human spot checks stay flat, prompts may have been tuned toward what the judge rewards. Periodic recalibration on fresh human labels detects both this and drift.

When a judge screens for a dangerous failure (missing medication information in discharge summaries), calibrate for recall on that failure against expert labels, set the threshold to favor recall, and keep sampling the cases it passes for human review. Average agreement can hide misses on rare, dangerous cases. When an uncalibrated judge passes everything, lowering the pass threshold makes it more permissive, not more sensitive. Calibration comes before any threshold change.

Judge items show agreement data, bias evidence or a gate that passes everything. Pick the step that establishes or restores calibration first: control the bias, re-measure against humans, fix the rubric, recalibrate after a model change, withhold gating authority. Distractors switch to a bigger judge, change the scale, lower thresholds, average inconsistent verdicts, or replace human labels with the judge.
