Online Quality Measurement. Measure quality on live traffic with representative sampling, A/B tests with planned duration and guardrails, shadow and canary evaluation, feedback loops into the evaluation suite, and metrics chosen for the task type.

Offline evaluation reduces the risk of a change; online measurement shows whether it helped real users. Live traffic brings inputs the suite never had, and changes that look neutral on one metric can hurt another, such as resolution rate unchanged but answers so long that users take longer to finish. Online quality measurement needs representative samples, sound experiments and metrics that fit the task.

- Random, across the whole day, stratified by key segments (region, route, tenant tier, language). Sampling the first conversations of each hour over-represents one time zone. - Large enough to detect the change that matters when comparing a release's cohort with the previous version's. - Within segments when traffic mix shifts: a 6% drop on the day a large customer onboards 4,000 users may be a population change, not a regression.

Task type Online metrics Extraction Field-level accuracy on sampled documents checked against verified values; downstream correction rate Retrieval-grounded Groundedness of sampled answers against the retrieved sources; no-evidence rate Agentic Share of work accepted without major rework; reverts or failures after acceptance; cost per successful task Generation Rubric pass rate from a calibrated judge; user effort (follow-ups, edits) Fluency ratings for structured fields, word counts and "mentions tests" are not quality metrics.

Thumbs up and down are valuable but sparse and self-selected (often 1 to 2% of users, skewed to frustrated ones). Use them to flag problems and find examples, alongside a sampled, rubric-based evaluation that estimates quality without that bias. Prompting users more often changes who responds, not the bias.

Practice Why Plan the duration to cover traffic cycles (for example two weeks) Weekday and weekend behavior differ Do not stop early when a variant looks good Peeking inflates false positives Declare a primary metric and guardrail metrics with limits before starting Prevents choosing the favorable metric afterward Check assignment balance across key segments A large tenant landing in one arm biases the result Combine outcomes into cost per successful outcome where trade-offs exist Makes completion versus escalation trade-offs explicit

To compare a candidate without exposing many users: - Shadow: run the candidate on live queries and score its answers offline without showing them. - Canary: a small share of traffic with guardrail metrics and automatic rollback. A full switch for a day, compared with the previous day, exposes everyone and confounds the result with the day.

docs.c: Offline gains are not online gains
docs.x: Flagged conversations go to a review queue where reviewers confirm the failure and its category; confirmed failures join the evaluation suite with the expected behavior written down. Adding every thumbs-down automatically adds noise and mislabels, and teams do not retrain Claude from their own feedback, so the loop improves prompts, tools and the suite. A change rated slightly better offline can be neutral on resolution and still cost users time. Confirm online, and include latency and user effort in the metrics.

Online-quality items describe a live measurement or experiment and a decision. Check the sample (representative?), the experiment (planned duration, guardrails, balance), and the metric (fits the task?). Distractors ship on one day's data, trust sparse ratings as the main metric, sample by convenience, measure fluency for extraction, or switch all traffic to compare.

Cost Architecture at Scale. Model and forecast cost per unit of work, route requests across the model family with validated routers and cascades, design caching from its break-even, move offline work to batch, enforce per-tenant budgets before requests run, and explain bills from usage data.

Fleet-level cost work starts from a breakdown, not a hunch. Spend is volume times cost per unit of work, and cost per unit is the sum of token categories at their prices, across the models each route uses. Most savings come from a few levers applied where the breakdown points: routing, caching, batch, right-sized outputs and context, and sensible defaults.

For each route, model cost per task (a claim, a conversation, a report) from its components: - steps per task and tokens per step, split into uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output; - the model each step uses; - retries, escalations and human handling for a full cost per successful outcome . Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens on Claude models, so verbose outputs can dominate even when inputs are larger. Then cost per unit changed. Break it down by token category and by model mix per route: more tokens per request, or routes moving to a higher tier.

Forecast cost per unit from its components, including planned features (two extra tool calls per claim), then multiply by forecast volume. Scaling last quarter's total by expected growth misses changes in cost per unit. Budget alerts should be forward-looking : project month-end spend from the current run rate, with an early-warning threshold.

Design Saves money when Fails when Router: classify each request and send it to the cheapest model that meets its floor The classifier is validated on evaluation data (for example 95% precision on "simple") The router is unvalidated, or routes by guesswork Cascade: try a small model, check the result, escalate failures Most items succeed on the cheap tier Escalation is frequent: at 45% escalation, every escalated item pays twice and the cascade costs more than going direct Escalate on failed checks , never on customer complaints.

Fact Consequence Reads cost a small fraction of input; writes cost more than input A prefix pays off after a small number of reuses within its lifetime The default lifetime is short (five minutes, renewed on use) Requests spaced further apart miss; the one-hour lifetime costs more to write, so check it against the actual reuse rate The cache matches an exact prefix: tools, system, messages Anything per-request before the breakpoint (timestamps, user IDs, tool order) creates a new entry every time A prefix below the model's minimum is not cached No error is raised; watch the usage fields Diagnose with cache reads as a share of input and cache-creation tokens over time (lesson 3.1).

Work with no one waiting (nightly classification, catalog generation, evaluation runs) belongs in the Message Batches API at a lower price per token, with the same model and quality. Work with a freshness or interactive requirement stays real time.

- Retrieved context: retrieve fewer, better-ranked passages, guided by recall measurements. - Programmatic tool calling: for many independent lookups, a script calls the tools and only its output reaches Claude, cutting tokens and round trips. It helps less when each step depends on reasoning over the last result, and it has its own billing and limits. - Defaults: most usage runs on defaults. A mid-tier default model and a moderate default effort, with escalation available, move most spend; bans and flat caps block valuable work.

Enforce budgets in the request path : check the tenant's remaining budget (using an estimated request cost) before forwarding, with soft limits as tenants approach it (warnings, slowing non-urgent work). Reconciling from the invoice or reading a console weekly does not cap anything.

Cost items give a breakdown, a bill that grew, or a proposed design. Find the largest driver and pick the lever for it, checking the economics (escalation rate, reuse within cache lifetime, latency needs). Distractors move everything to one tier, cap everyone flatly, compare per-request instead of per-outcome cost, or enforce budgets after the fact.

Latency Engineering. Break a Claude application's latency into its parts, tell time to first token from total latency, and apply the matching technique (streaming, parallel tool execution, cache checkpoints, effort tuning, model routing, shorter outputs) measured end to end.

"It is slow" can mean two different things. Time to first token (TTFT) is how long before anything appears; total latency is how long until the work is done. Users of a chat judge the first; users waiting on an agent task judge the second. Each has different causes and different fixes, so start from the target and the breakdown.

Component Affects Main levers Processing a long input before generation TTFT Cache the stable prefix; send less input Thinking before the answer TTFT of visible text Effort level; skip thinking for simple requests; summarized thinking display Generating output Total latency Shorter outputs where full length is not needed; faster model tier Sequential model calls in an agent loop Total latency Fewer turns; parallel tool calls; cached prefix on every call Tool and retrieval time Total latency Speed up, cache or parallelize the slow tool; rerank fewer candidates Waiting to display until done Perceived TTFT Streaming If a credit-check tool takes 8 of 14 seconds, switching models optimizes a minority of the time. Read the span breakdown before choosing a technique.

Streaming shows text as it is generated. It fixes a product that waits for the full response before displaying anything: if the first token arrives in 1.1 seconds but the page shows nothing for 9, streaming meets a "first text in 1.5 seconds" target. It does not reduce total generation time, cost or content.

When Claude requests several independent tools in one turn, run them concurrently in the harness and return all the results together in the next message. Executing three 1.2-second lookups one after another wastes the parallelism the model already offered. Asking Claude to call one tool per turn adds round trips.

A long, reused prefix (a 120,000-token contract, a stable system prompt and tool list) is processed much faster when it is read from the cache. This cuts TTFT for follow-up questions and speeds every call in an agent loop that re-sends the same prefix. Streaming does not shorten that processing; caching does.

Effort sets how much reasoning the model does. The highest effort on simple requests (renaming a variable) can mean 25 seconds of thinking before any output. Lower effort for request types that evaluation shows do not need deep reasoning, and keep higher effort where it improves results. With thinking enabled, the first visible text arrives after the thinking, which is why a streamed interface can stay blank for seconds.

Faster tiers usually return the first token sooner and generate faster. Route simple queries to a faster model where evaluation shows quality holds, keep complex ones on the current model, and measure latency per route. But measure per completed task : a faster model that causes more follow-up questions can make users' total time longer.

When a product has a first-response target (3 seconds) and a completion target (12 seconds), use different techniques for each: stream a short acknowledgment or plan quickly, then shorten the critical path with parallel tool calls and fewer turns. Capping output at 200 tokens makes responses finish faster by truncating the answers users came for. Right-size outputs by asking for shorter answers where full length is not needed.

Latency items give a target and a breakdown. Decide whether the target is TTFT or total, find the largest component, and pick the technique that acts on it. Distractors stream to cut total time, cache to cut generation time, raise effort, disable thinking everywhere, move everything to the smallest model, or truncate output.

Runtime Guardrail Systems. Layer guardrails to fit an agent's risk profile, with input and output filtering, PII redaction, hooks and permission rules, sandboxes, approval gates, refusal handling and deterministic limits on irreversible actions, and tune each layer for both false positives and false negatives.

No single guardrail is perfect, so production agents use layers, each catching what the others miss. The exam asks you to pick layers that fit a specific risk profile, and to tell advisory controls (prompts, instructions, CLAUDE.md) from enforced ones (code, permissions, hooks, sandboxes, gates). When the stakes are irreversible, the answer is enforced.

Layer What it does Example Input screening Detects prompt-injection patterns and policy violations in untrusted input Screening incoming emails before the agent reads them Redaction Masks PII at boundaries Card and social security numbers masked before logs and analytics Capability scoping The agent never holds what it should not use A read-only database role; no ownership-change tool Deterministic limits Hard rules in code Reject any transfer over $250,000, whatever the agent sends Hooks and permission rules Allow, deny or ask before a tool call runs A PreToolUse hook blocking destructive commands on protected paths Sandboxing Grants tool and network access without exposing production Egress only to the package registry; no production credentials Approval gates A person decides before an irreversible step Transfers over $10,000 or to new payees pause for an approver Output checks Catch leaks and violations before display or storage Internal data classes checked before a summary is shared Refusal handling A safe fallback when the model declines Replace partial streamed output with a helpful message; log for review Deleting shared data, moving money, changing ownership: use a capability the agent does not have, a hard limit, a blocking hook or an approval gate. A stronger system prompt is still a request, and logging after the fact only detects the damage.

docs.h: Hooks in Claude Code and the Agent SDK
docs.x: - PreToolUse runs before a tool call and is the enforcement point. Block with exit code 2 or a JSON permission decision of deny ; ask hands the decision to the user; updatedInput can rewrite the call (for example, redact a secret from a command). - Exit code 1 is non-blocking: the call runs. A hook meant to stop something must exit 2. - PostToolUse runs after the call: right for formatting, linting and logging, too late to prevent anything. - Stop can refuse to end the turn, for example until tests pass. Rules that must hold on every machine (no force-push to main) belong in managed settings as deny rules or hooks that engineers cannot override, not in CLAUDE.md or a wiki.

docs.h: Permission modes and what they guard
docs.x: Auto mode's classifier reviews actions for dangerous intent; it does not judge whether code is correct. Pair it with a Stop hook that runs the tests. Bypass permissions mode removes checks and belongs only inside isolated containers. Unattended runs use a mode that denies anything not pre-approved.

A sandbox grants exactly the access a task needs: network egress to an allowlist (the package registry), no production credentials, and OS-level limits on what shell commands can read. Tool-level deny rules on file tools do not stop a shell command reading a credentials file; the sandbox does.

Every filter has false positives (legitimate requests blocked) and false negatives (bad ones passed). Measure both on labeled samples of real traffic , per entity or category, and tune to the risk: - an input filter that blocks 8% of legitimate questions to catch 99% of attacks is costing users heavily; - a PII filter that masks medication doses makes clinical summaries useless, which is a clinical risk of its own; - refine detection (context-aware rather than keyword patterns), then confirm true positives are still caught. Adding keywords usually raises false positives; removing a filter entirely raises false negatives. Retrying a refusal on another model until one answers can bypass a legitimate safety decision. Detect refusals, show a safe fallback, and log them so over-refusals can be fixed in prompts.

Guardrail items describe an agent, its tools and a failure or risk. Choose the layer that would have prevented it, preferring enforced controls placed before the action, and check that the design does not add needless friction (gating everything) or remove the human step already relied on. Distractors strengthen prompts, log after the fact, use exit code 1, rely on auto mode for correctness, or add keywords.

List the layers you would put around the transfer tool, in the order a request meets them. 2. Decide what is enforced in code and what is advisory. 3. Design the redaction for card numbers. 4. Threat Defense and Adversarial Testing for Agentic Systems. Map the attack surface of tool-using agents (prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, exfiltration paths, unsafe autonomy, the combination of private data, untrusted input and external communication), defend in depth, design red-team exercises, and configure MCP securely, using OWASP and NIST guidance.

A chatbot that is manipulated says something wrong. A tool-using agent that is manipulated does something wrong: sends data out, changes records, spends money. Every source of text the agent reads (tickets, emails, web pages, PDFs, tool results, MCP tool descriptions, memory) is a possible channel for instructions an attacker wrote. Assume the model can be fooled; the controls must still hold.

Leg Examples Access to private data CRM records, internal wiki, accounts Exposure to untrusted input Customer tickets, web pages, uploaded documents, third-party tool output A channel to communicate externally Email, public posting, outbound HTTP, sharing links When all three meet in one context, prompt instructions alone cannot prevent exfiltration. Break a leg: scope data to the task (the ticket's own account), gate or remove the external channel (recipient allowlists, approval for external sends, no posting after internal reads), or narrow untrusted input (browsing allowlists).

docs.c: The memo that added a recipient
docs.x: Attack What happens Defenses Indirect prompt injection Instructions hidden in content the agent reads Separate untrusted content from capabilities; enforce actions in code; check outputs at trust boundaries Tool poisoning Hidden instructions in an MCP tool's description or output Review and pin tool definitions; alert on changes; egress limits Memory poisoning Injected text persisted into memory, steering later sessions Validate what may be written; scope memory; make entries reviewable Exfiltration Data leaves through email, URLs, posts or tool calls Allowlisted destinations; approval for external sends; output checks Unsafe autonomy The agent takes costly or irreversible actions unchecked Least privilege, quotas, approval gates System prompt leakage Users extract the prompt Keep secrets and sensitive details out of prompts A transaction memo told Granite's fraud agent to add an external address to a case's notification list. The fix was not a better prompt: changing notification recipients was removed from the agent's capabilities and left to analysts.

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications names the risk categories, including prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency (more functionality, permissions or autonomy than needed), system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption. An agent that launched 300 instances in a loop after misreading an error is an excessive-agency problem: limits, quotas and approvals bound the damage whatever triggers it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes the work into four functions: Govern (policies, roles, accountability), Map (context and risk identification), Measure (assessment and tracking) and Manage (prioritizing and responding). Its Generative AI Profile applies the framework to risks specific to generative systems.

docs.h: Red-team exercises that change the system

- Allow only reviewed servers , from approved sources, with pinned versions . - Give each server least-privilege credentials and enable only the tools agents need. - Record tool-definition hashes and alert when a server's descriptions change. - Being listed in a public directory is not a trust decision.

Require a human when an action is irreversible or costly , or when untrusted content has entered the session and the action sends data outside . Length, user tenure and time of day are not risk properties.

Threat items describe an agent's tools and inputs and an attack or near miss. Identify which legs of the combination are present and which channel carried the attack, then pick the structural control that closes the path. Distractors strengthen prompts, enlarge models, encrypt data the agent still reads, filter keywords, log after the fact, or trust listed servers.

Tide reads each tenant's uploaded documents, queries metrics, creates reports and can share a report with any email address. 140 tenants enable a third-party CRM MCP server. Tenants can upload documents written by their own customers. 1. Map the three legs of the high-risk combination for Tide. 2. Identify two attack paths and the channel each uses. 3. Propose structural controls that close each path. 4. Design one red-team scenario and say what makes it pass. 1. Legs. Private data: tenant documents and metrics. Untrusted input: uploaded documents written by tenants' customers, CRM tool output and tool descriptions. External channel: share_report to any email address. 2. Paths. - An uploaded document contains instructions to create a report of sensitive metrics and share it to an outside address (indirect injection through documents, exfiltration through share_report ). - The CRM server's tool description is changed to tell Tide to include the tenant's documents in a CRM note (tool poisoning, exfiltration through the CRM tool). 3. Identity, Secrets, and Audit at Scale. Give each agent its own identity and least-privilege credentials, replace static API keys with workload identity federation, keep secrets out of the model's context, authorize per user, and write audit events from the systems that execute actions.

Agents act on real systems, so they need the same identity discipline as any other workload, and a little more, because a manipulated agent will use whatever access it holds. The principles are familiar: distinct identities, short-lived credentials, least privilege, secrets out of reach, and an audit trail written by the system that did the work.

Practice Why Each agent gets its own identity, distinct from humans and other agents Actions are attributable to a specific agent Credentials are per agent, short-lived and rotated automatically A leak is contained in time and scope Permissions follow the agent's role Compromise of one agent does not expose everything Agents never grant themselves permissions Self-escalation defeats least privilege A shared service account for all agents makes attribution impossible and turns one leak into an organization-wide exposure.

Static API keys in pipelines are long-lived secrets copied into many places; when one leaks, rotation means coordinating every copy. Workload identity federation lets a workload (a CI job, a service) exchange its own platform identity for short-lived credentials, so there is no stored key to leak or rotate, and access is scoped and revocable per workload. Rotating a static key weekly shortens exposure but keeps a leakable secret.

docs.h: Secrets stay out of the context
docs.x: A secret in a system prompt can leak through outputs, logs and traces, whatever the prompt says about keeping it. Keep secrets in a secrets manager , used by tool code on the server side: the model receives the capability (the tool), never the credential. Encoding a secret is not protecting it, and letting the agent fetch the secret itself still puts it in the context.

- Scope data to the user and task, enforced by the backend: a CRM tool that serves the authenticated customer's records only. - Grant the operations the job needs: read-only when the agent only answers questions. - Scope credentials to the resources used: a GitHub token for the three repositories the agent works on, not the whole organization. - Authorize per user on MCP servers that act for users: authenticate each user and authorize each tool call against that user's permissions, while the server's own downstream credentials stay narrow.

For Claude Code across an organization, configure authentication centrally in managed settings (the organization's account, or an LLM gateway that holds the credentials), so engineers never handle provider keys. Managed settings can restrict permission rules and hooks to those the organization deploys and block local overrides, so policies cannot be bypassed with launch flags.

An audit event answers: who (agent and the user it acted for), did what (action and parameters), to which target , under which approval , when , and with what outcome . Three rules: 1. Write it from the system that executes the action (the tool or backend), not from the agent describing it. An agent can skip a logging call or write a misleading entry. 2. Link approvals: the action's audit event references the approval system's record, so "which manager approved this refund?" is provable. 3. Log successful actions too. Auditors review what happened, not only what failed. Full conversation transcripts are not an audit record: hard to query, and full of content that may not belong in long-term storage. "Rotate the key monthly" and "encrypt the key in each repository" keep the underlying problem, a long-lived secret in many places. Federation removes it.

Identity items describe how agents authenticate, what they can reach and what is logged, then a leak, an over-broad grant or an audit gap. Choose the change that removes the long-lived secret, narrows the grant, moves authorization to the backend, or makes the audit record authoritative. Distractors rotate, encrypt, share accounts, put secrets or user lists in prompts, or rely on agreements and reviews.

Parallel Agent Orchestration for Engineering Work. Fan large engineering work out to parallel coding agents on isolated worktrees, decompose it so branches rarely conflict, land shared changes first, resolve conflicts with both intents in view, pace the fleet to review capacity, and read fleet telemetry for shared failure causes.

Coding agents make it cheap to start many streams of work at once. Throughput then depends on three things: whether the streams interfere with each other, whether their branches merge cleanly, and whether review keeps up. The exam tests each of those, plus reading fleet telemetry for failures that look random one agent at a time.

A parallel session is a separate Claude Code instance working its own task, usually in its own worktree. A subagent is a helper inside one session, with its own context and tools, for jobs such as exploration or verification. Parallel sessions raise the number of tasks in flight; subagents keep each session focused.

Six sessions in one checkout overwrite each other's edits, and tests see files change mid-run. A worktree gives each session its own checkout on its own branch ( claude --worktree <name> ), and the branches are merged afterward through normal review. Worktrees start from the repository, so git-ignored files a session needs (a local environment file) are missing; list them in .worktreeinclude to copy them in, rather than committing secrets.

Practice Why Give each task its own set of files, such as one service per task Independent file sets rarely conflict Land shared changes first (a library wrapper, a common interface) in one task Parallel tasks build on one version instead of each editing it Keep tasks that share files in one session, one after another Coupled edits conflict when split Start every task from the current main A stale base spreads the same failure across many branches Random grouping can put coupled code in different tasks. Letting every agent edit shared code "and resolve differences at the end" guarantees conflicts.

When two branches change the same file in different ways, resolve it in one session that reads both branches' intent, then run the full tests. Accepting whichever branch merged first can silently break the other feature; re-running tasks until one avoids the file does not resolve conflicting requirements.

Generation can outpace review. If 300 pull requests a week sit longer and longer while approval rates hold, review capacity is the bottleneck , and adding agents makes the queue longer. Limit sessions per engineer to what they can review properly (two or three is a sensible start), pace fan-out to the review rate, and scale verification and AI review (lesson 8.2).

Verification and AI Code Review Operations. When agents write code faster than people can review it, give agents feedback loops that verify their own work, protect the checks from the agent, introduce AI code review in shadow mode and calibrate it against human review before it gates merges, and keep a human approver.

When generation outpaces review, the reviewer becomes the bottleneck, and the temptation is to trust summaries, skip review for small changes or let automated review approve. Verification operations keep quality while throughput grows: the agent checks its own work before anyone sees it, the checks cannot be weakened by the agent, AI review earns authority through calibration, and a human stays accountable.

Give every session a way to verify its own work before reporting done: - one command for tests and one for the build, each exiting non-zero on failure, listed in CLAUDE.md with examples of healthy output; - a quantifiable target ("all tests in test_status.py pass"); - for UI work, a browser or screenshot tool and a mock to compare against; - for bug fixes, write the failing test first , confirm it fails for the expected reason, commit it, and only then ask for the fix.

An agent fixing code must not be able to weaken the check on that code. A fix that edits a failing test's expected value to match buggy output "passes". Prevent it with a hook that blocks edits to test files during fix tasks , or reject any fix that touches the test in review. An instruction in CLAUDE.md is advisory. Make tests a gate, not a promise : a Stop hook runs the suite and refuses to end the turn on failure (exit 2 feeds the failure back so the agent fixes it), and a PostToolUse hook lints and type-checks after edits.

How the run happened Verification Watched closely in a short session A quick read of the diff Unattended, overnight or in CI Start from the diff, not the summary ; check the JSON result and exit status; tests enforced by hook; a fresh reviewer (a separate session with no memory of writing the code) for anything that matters A tidy summary can hide a change to a file nobody expected the agent to touch. Small changes can still break critical paths.

docs.h: AI code review: from shadow to gate
docs.x: Stage What happens Moves on when Shadow AI review runs on every pull request; findings are compared with human reviews Precision and recall are measured Advisory Findings posted for authors and reviewers Engineers act on them; noise is low Gate Severity counts feed a merge rule the team builds Precision on blocking-level findings is acceptable, and recall on serious defects is known Two measures decide gating: precision of the findings that would block (share confirmed real by humans) and recall on serious defects (share of human-found serious issues it also found). Comment volume, speed and unverified opinions do not. A managed AI review service posts ranked findings; it does not approve, block or push fixes. Teams keep branch protection and code-owner approval, and can build a merge gate on its findings once they trust them.

If many findings are style comments, engineers stop reading all of them, including real bugs. Tune the review policy: reserve high severity for defects that would break behavior, leak data or breach policy; cap low-priority comments; exclude generated files and what CI already enforces. When review flags the same mistake twice, add the correction to CLAUDE.md so the next pull request avoids it.

docs.h: Human oversight and separation of duties
docs.x: The agent that wrote the code cannot approve it. Branch protection requires a human code owner , and no agent identity can approve or merge its own pull requests. Engineers who directed the agent are its authors in effect and should not self-approve. Tests and AI review inform the approval; they do not replace it.

Verification items describe a pipeline where agents produce lots of code, and a quality problem or a proposal to automate review. Pick the control that verifies before humans look, protects the check, calibrates AI review before giving it authority, or keeps a human approver distinct from the author. Distractors trust summaries, make AI review required on day one, let it approve, skip review for small diffs, or rely on CLAUDE.md rules.

docs.h: Apply it: Calibrate Riverbend's AI code review
docs.x: Riverbend's managed AI review runs on 60 repositories but is not a required check. Engineers mark 46% of its findings "not useful", mostly style comments. Agent-authored pull requests have a first-pass CI success rate of 64%. The VP wants AI review to block merges within a quarter. 1. Design the shadow-mode study and what it measures. 2. Tune the review policy to fix the noise. 3. Improve agents' first-pass success before code reaches review. 4. State the conditions for gating, and what stays human. 1. Shadow study. For six weeks, compare AI findings with human review on 400 pull requests across 10 representative repositories. A tech lead labels each AI finding as confirmed or not, and each human-found serious defect as caught or missed by the AI. Report precision by severity and recall on serious defects, by repository type. 2. Policy. Update REVIEW.md: severity "Important" only for defects that break behavior, leak data or breach policy; style findings are nits, capped at five per review and summarized; generated paths and anything CI enforces are excluded. Mistakes flagged twice go into CLAUDE.md. 3. First-pass success. Each repository's CLAUDE.md lists one test command and one build command with healthy output; a Stop hook runs the tests before an agent can finish; bug-fix tasks start from a committed failing test with test-file edits blocked by a hook. 4. Gating. AI review blocks only on "Important" findings, and only in repository types where shadow precision on those findings is at least the agreed level (for example 85%) and recall on serious defects is known. A human code owner still approves every pull request, and no agent can approve or merge its own. - AI review is measured against human review before it gets authority. - Noise is reduced by policy, not by ignoring findings. - Agents verify their own work, and the checks are protected. - A human approver stays distinct from the author.

Unattended and Event-Driven Agent Operations. Run coding agents without a person watching, whether toward a goal, on a schedule or in response to events such as CI failures, with permission modes that never wait, checkable completion conditions, checkpoints, structured output, notification and escalation, and bounded authority.

Unattended agents do recurring or triggered engineering work with nobody watching each step: a nightly dependency audit, a weekly report, a first diagnosis of every failed build, a multi-hour upgrade toward "all tests pass". With no person in the loop, the design must answer what a person would: when to stop, what to do when stuck, who to tell, and what the agent may never do on its own.

Shape Trigger Examples Goal-driven Started once, runs until a condition holds Upgrade a framework until tests pass and the type checker is clean Scheduled A schedule, an HTTP call or a repository event Daily audit, weekly stale-PR report, triage of new issues Event-driven responder An alert or CI failure Read the failed build's logs, diagnose, propose a fix

Option Fits when Cloud scheduled tasks Same prompt on a recurring trigger, no need for your network; nothing to host (runs at most hourly, starts from a fresh clone) Headless Claude Code ( claude -p ) in CI or cron The job needs your environment or pipeline Agent SDK service The work belongs inside your own product or webhook service

An unattended run that hits a permission prompt hangs until the job times out. Run with a non-interactive permission mode that denies anything not pre-approved , and list exactly the tools the job needs. Bypass permissions mode removes the safety net and belongs only in isolated containers.

- Declare the configuration: skip auto-discovered local configuration and pass the settings and MCP config the job needs, so every runner starts the same. (Skipping discovery also skips CLAUDE.md, Skills and hooks, so do not use it where those are what is being tested.) - Bound the loop with a maximum number of turns and a budget. - Return structured output: JSON constrained by a schema, read by the next script, instead of free text parsed with regular expressions. - Chain stages by session ID: capture it from the first run's JSON output and resume that session for the second stage, rather than pasting a plan into a fresh session.

A goal needs a completion condition that can be checked from the run's output (the test results), not the agent's belief that it is done. Add checkpoints (commits at safe points) so progress survives interruptions, and notify the owner on completion or when the run is stuck, with a summary. No self-merging: the result arrives as a pull request through review.

A CI first responder starts on the failure event, investigates with read access and narrowly scoped tools (no production credentials), posts its diagnosis in the team channel, and opens any fix as a pull request through normal review. It does not push to main or skip failing jobs. For responders driven by metrics, put deterministic detection first: control bands and run rules so only sustained or extreme readings trigger action, tiers (log, diagnose read-only, act through pre-approved runbooks only), and a cap on automated actions per period with escalation to a person when it is reached. A noisy metric that triggers 20 rollbacks in a night needs better detection and a cap, not a responder that widens its own thresholds.

docs.c: The agent decides it is done
docs.x: Scheduled agents are stateless unless the design gives them state. A triage job that runs every 15 minutes and asks maintainers the same question repeatedly needs a durable record of what it handled and asked, read at the start of each run. A completion condition that relies on the agent saying the work is finished, or on a magic word in the output, is not a check. Use the test results, exit status and structured fields.

Unattended-operation items describe a job that hangs, loops, repeats itself, breaks a downstream script, acts too often or acts without review. Choose the control that makes it non-interactive, bounded, checkable, stateful, structured, notified or gated. Distractors use bypass mode, raise timeouts, rely on someone watching, remove limits, let agents merge or widen their own thresholds.

docs.h: Apply it: Design Riverbend's CI first responder
docs.x: Riverbend wants its CI first responder to handle every failed main-branch build: read the logs, decide whether the failure is flaky or real, find the likely cause, and propose a fix. Today the job sometimes hangs on permission prompts, sometimes posts long free-text messages nobody reads, and once retried a flaky test 30 times in an hour. 1. Specify how the job runs: trigger, permission mode and tools. 2. Define the output it produces and where it goes. 3. Bound its authority and its activity. 4. Design state and escalation so it does not repeat itself or go unnoticed. 1. Running. Triggered by the CI failure event on main. Headless Claude Code with a non-interactive mode that denies anything not pre-approved; allowed tools: read files, gh run view for logs, git log , and creating a branch and draft pull request. A turn limit of 25 and a budget per run. 2. Output. JSON matching a schema: verdict (flaky, real, unknown), failing_test , suspected_commit , evidence (log lines), proposed_fix (a draft pull request link or none). A script posts a three-line summary in the owning team's channel with the links. 3. Bounds. No push to main, no merge, no re-running or skipping jobs, no production credentials. For flaky verdicts, at most one re-run of the job per failure; any further action is a pull request that quarantines the test, through review. 4. State and escalation. A record per failing test (last verdict, actions taken, pull requests opened) is read at the start of each run, so the same test is not diagnosed again within the hour. If a "real" failure has no proposed fix after two runs, or main has been red for 60 minutes, the on-call engineer is paged with the summary. - The job never waits for input and is bounded in turns and budget. - Output is structured and delivered where people act on it. - Authority stops at draft pull requests and one re-run. - Durable state prevents repeats, and escalation has a clear trigger.

Organization-Wide Coding Agent Configuration. Configure coding agents for a whole organization with managed settings that cannot be overridden, MCP allowlists, sandboxes, central telemetry and gateway routing, sensible model defaults, and a quality and safety bar for sharing prompts, Skills, plugins and MCP servers across teams.

When hundreds of engineers run coding agents, individual configuration stops being enough. Policies that must hold everywhere need central enforcement; shared workflows need a way to spread without copying files; usage needs to be visible; and the components teams share (prompts, Skills, plugins, MCP servers) need a bar before they reach everyone.

Managed settings are deployed centrally (device management or the admin console) and take precedence over user, project and local settings. They are where non-negotiable policy lives: Setting area Typical policy Permission deny rules No reading secret files; no force-push to main; no arbitrary network tools Bypass mode disabled No engineer can switch off permission checks Managed-only permission rules and hooks Local settings and launch flags cannot widen rules or disable gates MCP allowlist (managed MCP servers only) Only approved servers load in any session Plugin marketplace restrictions Plugins install only from approved marketplaces Sandbox required for shell commands Credential files and environment variables denied; fail to start if the sandbox is unavailable Minimum version Sessions refuse to start on an unapproved version A shared .claude/settings.json in each repository is a team convenience, not enforcement: user and local settings can override it. A security guide or a quarterly review of settings files does not enforce anything.

Permission rules govern Claude's own tools. A shell command run by Claude can still read a cloud credentials file unless the sandbox denies it. Require the sandbox to be available, so sessions fail to start rather than silently running unsandboxed.

- Telemetry: enable OpenTelemetry export through managed settings to the organization's collector, so every session reports usage, cost and tool decisions; prompt text stays out unless explicitly enabled. - Gateway routing: route traffic through an LLM gateway that holds credentials, enforces quotas and logs usage. The gateway must forward the headers and endpoints Claude Code uses; feature-specific failures after enabling one usually trace to header handling.

Most usage runs on defaults. Set a sensible default model and effort level centrally, with per-role overrides where work needs more, and adjust from usage and cost data. Forcing the smallest model for everything blocks hard tasks; no defaults at all tends to make the most expensive settings the norm.

Packaging beats copying. Plugins bundle Skills, subagents, hooks and MCP configuration as versioned, installable units distributed through an internal marketplace; managed settings restrict installation to approved marketplaces. A plugin runs code with the engineer's privileges and its hooks fire on matching tool calls, so review it before approving it, and remember that being listed in a public marketplace is not a trust decision. The bar for sharing a Skill, prompt or MCP server company-wide: Requirement Why An evaluation showing it beats the baseline on realistic cases, including edge cases Evidence it helps, not just that it works for its author A security review of what it can access and run Shared components run everywhere A named owner and versioning Someone updates it when policy or APIs change Popularity, a senior engineer's approval or "it works on my machine" are not a bar. A community plugin's Stop hook called an external URL on every turn. With marketplace restrictions in managed settings, it could not have been installed; with sandbox egress limits, its calls would have failed.

Organization-configuration items describe a policy, a bypass or a sharing problem across many engineers. Pick the central, enforced mechanism (managed settings, sandbox, allowlists, marketplace restrictions, gateway, telemetry export) or the evidence-based sharing bar. Distractors rely on repository files, guides, agreements, onboarding steps, periodic reviews, emailed zip files or public listings.

Rate limit, refusal or length stop; recall, ranking or generation; model, harness, tool or data. 3. Enforce outside the model. Limits, permissions, hooks, gates and sandboxes, not prompt instructions, when stakes are real. 4. Mitigate first, diagnose second. A tested rollback or a narrow flag before the root cause is known. 5. Measure the instrument. Judges against human labels, gates with repeated trials, metrics by segment. 6. Change one thing, then measure. The narrowest fix at the layer that failed.

AWS's managed service for foundation models, through which Claude can be used inside an AWS account. Also: Bedrock
A record of who did what and when, including an agent's actions and tool calls, kept for review, compliance and investigating incidents. Also: audit logs, audit trail
A systematic skew in output, such as favoring certain groups, viewpoints or answer positions. Found by testing varied inputs and reviewing the results. Also: biased
Splitting documents into smaller passages for indexing and retrieval. Chunk size and where the boundaries fall decide what retrieval can find. Also: chunk, chunks
A safeguard that stops calling a failing tool or service after repeated errors, so the system fails fast instead of piling up retries. Also: circuit breakers
References from Claude's answer to the exact source passages behind it, so a reader can check each claim. Also: citation, cite sources
Anthropic's library, for Python and TypeScript, for building agents on the same agent loop, tools and context management that power Claude Code. Also: Agent SDK
Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads code, edits files and runs commands, in the terminal, an IDE, the desktop app or the browser.
Anthropic's hosted service that runs agents in a managed sandbox, with sessions and events, so you do not have to build and operate the agent loop yourself. Also: Managed Agents
A Markdown file that Claude Code loads at the start of a session, holding instructions such as build commands and coding conventions. It can be set for the user, the project or a single directory.
Summarizing the earlier part of a long conversation to free space in the context window while keeping the facts still needed. Also: compact, auto-compact
How well a stated confidence matches real accuracy. Well-calibrated scores can be used to send low-confidence cases to a person. Also: calibration, calibrated, well-calibrated

The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can consider in one request: the system prompt, the conversation so far, tool definitions and results, and its own reply. Whatever does not fit is not seen. Also: context length
An Anthropic technique that adds a short explanation of where each chunk fits in its document before the chunk is embedded and keyword-indexed, which cuts the number of failed retrievals.
A request setting that tells the model how much reasoning and how many tokens to spend, trading answer quality against speed and cost.
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text, so texts with similar meaning have nearby embeddings. Used for semantic search. Also: embeddings
Routing a case from the automated system to a person, triggered by rules such as low confidence, high value, a policy exception or the customer asking for one. Also: escalate, escalated, escalates

A repeatable test of a model, prompt or agent against a set of cases with expected outcomes, scored by code, by people or by a model. Used to compare versions and catch regressions. Also: eval, evals, evaluation, evaluations
Giving an AI system more functions, permissions or autonomy than its job needs, so a mistake or a manipulated instruction can do real damage.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt before retrying, usually with some random jitter, so retries do not overload the service. Also: backoff, retry with backoff

A mode in which Claude reasons step by step in thinking blocks before giving its final answer, within a token budget. It helps on complex, multi-step problems at the cost of extra tokens and time. Also: thinking budget, thinking blocks
A second working directory on its own branch of the same repository, so several Claude Code sessions can work in parallel without touching each other's files. Also: worktree, worktrees
A curated set of test cases with known correct answers that evaluations are scored against. Also: golden set, gold set, ground truth
Telling Claude to base its answer only on material you supply, and to say plainly when that material does not cover the question. Also: grounded
A check outside the model's own judgment that blocks or corrects unsafe or invalid actions, such as input validation, an allow list or a hook. Also: guardrails
Passing a task, together with the context needed to continue it, from one agent to another or from an agent to a person. Also: handoffs, hand off
Running Claude Code without the interactive session, using the -p flag, for scripts and CI pipelines. Output can be plain text or JSON.

A command that runs automatically at a set point in an agent's lifecycle, for example before a tool call (PreToolUse) or after it (PostToolUse). Unlike an instruction in a prompt, a hook always runs. Also: hooks, PreToolUse, PostToolUse

A design in which a person reviews or approves certain actions or outputs before they take effect, usually the high-impact or low-confidence ones. Also: human-in-the-loop, HITL, human review, human approval
Combining keyword search, such as BM25, with embedding search, so both exact terms like product codes and differently worded passages are found. Also: BM25

The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. An idempotency key lets an agent retry a write, such as a payment, without making it twice. Also: idempotent, idempotency key, idempotency keys
Improving a prompt or an output over several rounds, changing one thing at a time and checking the effect of each change. Also: iterate, iterating, iterative
The time between sending a request and getting the response. For chat, the time to the first token matters most. Also: time to first token, TTFT
Giving an agent or tool only the permissions its task needs, which limits the damage a mistake or an attack can do. Also: least-privilege

Using a model to grade another model's outputs against a rubric. Its grades need checking against human ones, because judges have biases such as preferring longer answers or the first answer shown. Also: LLM-as-judge, LLM judge, LLM-as-a-judge, model-graded
A proxy between applications, or Claude Code, and model providers that centralizes authentication, usage tracking, cost controls and routing. Also: LLM gateways, AI gateway
A Messages API feature that connects a request to remote MCP servers directly, without running your own MCP client.
A program that offers tools, resources or prompts over MCP, for example in front of a database, a file system or a business application. Also: MCP servers
A tool that lets Claude save and read information in files outside its context window, so knowledge can carry over between sessions.

An API for submitting large groups of requests that are processed asynchronously, usually within 24 hours, at half the normal price. Suited to work that does not need an answer straight away. Also: Batch API, batch processing, Message Batches
The main Claude API: you send a conversation as a list of user and assistant messages, plus optional system prompt and tools, and receive the next assistant message.

Restricting retrieval to documents whose metadata, such as date, product, region or access rights, matches the request, before or alongside similarity search. Also: metadata filters, metadata filtering
An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server offers tools, resources and prompts; an MCP client inside the application connects to it. Also: MCP
Moving an application to a newer model: rerunning evaluations, adjusting prompts and settings, and rolling the change out gradually. Also: migrating to a new model, model upgrade
Several agents, usually an orchestrator and specialized subagents, working on one task. It gains parallel work and separate contexts at the cost of more tokens and coordination. Also: multi-agent

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework, which organizes AI risk work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Also: AI Risk Management Framework, NIST AI Risk Management Framework
Being able to see what a system is doing from its traces, logs and metrics, such as each model call, tool call, delay and cost in an agent run. Also: tracing, traces
The agent or code that splits a task, hands the parts to workers or subagents and combines what they return. Also: coordinator, lead agent, orchestrator-workers
A widely used list of the most critical security risks for applications built on language models, such as prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency. Also: OWASP
The Claude Code setting for how much Claude may do without asking, from asking before every edit or command to accepting edits automatically. Plan mode is one of the modes. Also: permission modes

Information that can identify a person, such as a name, address, ID number or health record. Often removed or masked before text reaches a model or a log. Also: personally identifiable information, personal data
A package that bundles Claude Code extensions, such as skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers, so a team can install them together. Also: plugins
A catalog, usually a repository with a marketplace file, from which users find and install plugins. Also: marketplace
A judge's tendency to prefer an answer because of where it appears, first or second. Countered by running the comparison in both orders.
Precision is the share of flagged items that really are positive; recall is the share of real positives that were flagged. Raising one usually lowers the other.
Letting Claude write code that calls tools inside a code execution environment, so intermediate results are handled in code instead of passing through the context window.

Reusing the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix, such as long instructions or a reference document, across requests. Cached reads cost much less and return faster, but only an exact match of the prefix up to the cache breakpoint is reused. Also: cache breakpoint, cache_control

An attack in which instructions hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page, email, document or tool result, try to make it act against its user or developer. Also: indirect prompt injection, injection
A reusable prompt with fixed instructions and placeholders for the parts that change, so a team gets consistent results from the same kind of request. Also: prompt templates, template, templates
A cap on requests or tokens per minute for an organization. Going over it returns HTTP 429, which a client should handle by waiting and retrying with backoff. Also: rate limits, HTTP 429, 429
Running an evaluation suite again after a change, such as a new prompt, model or tool, to confirm that what worked before still works. Also: regression test, regression tests, regression suite
A second pass that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance, usually with a stronger model, so only the best few go into the prompt. Also: reranker, rerank
Fetching relevant passages from a knowledge source when a question arrives and placing them in the prompt, so the answer is grounded in that content rather than in the model's memory. Also: RAG
Running commands in an isolated environment with limits on file system and network access, so an agent can act with fewer approval prompts at lower risk. Also: sandbox, sandboxed

Information whose exposure could harm people or the organization, such as personal, financial, health or client-confidential data. It belongs only in approved tools, and only as much as the task needs. Also: confidential data, confidential information, sensitive information
Claude Code's configuration file, at user, project and local level, for permissions, hooks, environment variables and other options.

A folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions, plus optional scripts and resources, that Claude loads only when a task needs it. Skills work in Claude Code, the API and claude.ai. Also: skills, Agent Skills, SKILL.md

The field in an API response that says why generation ended, for example end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence or tool_use. An agent loop reads it to decide whether to run a tool or finish. Also: stop_reason, end_turn
Sampling from each category, such as document type or risk level, so that rare but important cases are checked too. Also: stratified sample
Receiving a response in pieces, as server-sent events, while it is being generated, so users see output at once instead of waiting for the whole message.
Constraining a response to a given JSON schema so code can parse it reliably. A tool with an input schema can be used the same way. Also: structured output
An agent started by another agent to handle one subtask in its own context window. It returns only its result, which keeps the parent's context small. Also: subagents, sub-agent
Instructions sent separately from the conversation that set Claude's role, rules and background for every turn of it. Also: system prompts
The unit models read and write text in, on average a little less than one English word. Context windows, rate limits and prices are all counted in tokens. Also: tokens

The text in a tool definition that says what the tool does, when to use it and what its inputs mean. Claude picks tools mainly from these descriptions, so vague or overlapping ones cause wrong choices. Also: tool descriptions
The message that returns a tool's output to Claude, matched to the request by its ID. Marking it as an error lets Claude see that the call failed and recover. Also: tool_result, is_error

Letting Claude call functions you define. Claude returns a tool_use request with arguments, your code runs the tool, and you send the output back as a tool result. Also: function calling, tool call, tool calls, tool calling

Checking AI output against a trusted reference before it is used, such as the source documents, known data or an expert, with more checking where the stakes are higher. Also: verify, verified, fact-check, fact-checking
Google Cloud's AI platform, through which Claude can be used inside a Google Cloud project. Also: Google Vertex AI, Google Cloud Vertex AI
Letting a workload authenticate with short-lived credentials from its own cloud identity provider instead of a long-lived API key stored with it.

An arrangement for eligible organizations under which prompts and outputs are not stored after the response is returned, apart from what the law or the arrangement requires. Also: ZDR, zero data retention
